cases.title: Seated Man with a Cane (1918)
cases.institution: New York Supreme Court; Geneva freeport (current location of painting)
cases.description: After an 11-year legal battle, NY Supreme Court Judge Joel M. Cohen ruled April 3, 2026 that billionaire art dealer David Nahmad must return Modigliani's Seated Man with a Cane (1918) to the estate of Oscar Stettiner, a Jewish antiques dealer whose Paris gallery was looted during the Nazi occupation. Nahmad's Panamanian holding company, International Art Center S.A., purchased the painting at Christie's London in 1996 for £2M; it has been in a Geneva freeport since. The Panama Papers (2016) revealed Nahmad as the holding company's sole owner after years of denial. Cohen found the painting identical to the looted work and that Stettiner 'never voluntarily relinquished it.' He criticized Christie's 1996 provenance catalog as 'flawed and misleading — whether by error or design.' On May 5, Nahmad filed a motion to review, citing a newly published Modigliani catalogue raisonné by Marc Restellini and eyewitness testimony claiming Mondex misidentified the painting.
cases.outcome: Ruling entered April 3, 2026 ordering return. Nahmad filed motion to review May 5. Return not yet executed. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING]
cases.tags: Repatriation, Legal challenge, Art market, Authenticity, Geopolitics
cases.notes: [FOLLOW-UP PENDING] Ruling missed in April sessions — retroactive parent entry. The Panama Papers connection is teachable for ARTH 201: the offshore freeport system that enabled Nahmad to obscure ownership for 20 years while a Nazi-looted painting sat in Geneva's tax-free warehouse is the financialization-of-art theme at its most concrete. Judge Cohen's criticism of Christie's 1996 provenance parallels entry 056 (Wildenstein/Monet) — both involve auction houses whose due diligence enabled contested works to enter the market. Restellini told The Art Newspaper he had 'serious doubts' about a provenance link and suggested thorough investigation — neither confirming nor denying the Nahmad motion. Connects to entries 061 (US-Italy repatriation), 035 (French repatriation law). Theme 5 and Theme 10 both apply.
cases.interested_parties: Judge Joel M. Cohen (NYSSC); Philippe Maestracci (Stettiner's grandson, claimant); James Palmer / Mondex (restitution specialists); David Nahmad (defendant); International Art Center S.A. (Nahmad holding company); Christie's (criticized for 1996 provenance); Marc Restellini (catalogue raisonné author); Geri S. Krauss and Philip Landrigan (Stettiner counsel); ICIJ / Panama Papers
cases.coverage_geography: US, France, UK, Europe, global arts press

cases.title: The Migrant Child (2019)
cases.institution: Palazzo San Pantalon, Venice; Arsenale Tesa 113 (unveiling); Venice canals (boat tour)
cases.description: Banksy's 2019 Venice mural depicting a child refugee in a life vest holding a pink flare — painted illegally on Palazzo San Pantalon in the Santa Croce district — was removed from the deteriorated facade in July 2025 after years of saltwater damage eliminated roughly a third of the image. Banca Ifis, which acquired the palazzo in 2024 at the Italian Ministry of Culture's request, funded and supervised a full conservation-restoration by Federico Borgogni. The restored work was unveiled May 7 at Tesa 113 in the Arsenale during the Biennale Arte 2026 preview, then toured Venice's canals by boat May 8–9. Banca Ifis says it consulted people close to Banksy but could not confirm direct artist permission. The 2023 decision to restore the work rather than allow it to decay in situ generated debate among street art purists. The work is one of only two officially attributed Banksy pieces in Italy. Banca Ifis also launched an educational initiative, Migrant Child – Rights at Work, for Italian secondary schools in 2026–27.
cases.outcome: Restoration complete. Work unveiled May 7. Canal boat tour May 8–9. Return to Palazzo San Pantalon pending.
cases.tags: Conservation, Unauthorized public art, Removal, Migration, Protest art
cases.notes: [FOLLOW-UP PENDING: permanent installation location not confirmed — will work return to the palazzo facade or be installed indoors?] The Venice Biennale timing is deliberate — the work about migration tours the canals of a city whose lagoon migrants have drowned attempting to cross while the Biennale's most-contested controversies involve Palestine and Gaza. The Banksy conservation paradox is present here: the Italian state's decision to restore and preserve an illegally placed work, without the artist's explicit permission, is itself a governance of public art story. The boat-canal tour format — bringing the work to passersby rather than asking them to seek it — echoes Banksy's own street practice. Compare to entry 062/062-A (Banksy London Waterloo Place statue, retained by Westminster Council) as a paired 2026 Banksy case study on how institutions absorb and domesticate street art.
cases.interested_parties: Banca Ifis / Ernesto Fürstenberg Fassio (president); Federico Borgogni (conservator); Italy Ministry of Culture; Veneto Region President Luca Zaia; Kailash Satyarthi (2014 Nobel Peace Prize winner, present at unveiling); Banksy (artist; consulted indirectly)

cases.title: Tatlin's Whisper #6 / Fall of Freedom (national arts resistance platform)
cases.institution: Times Square (Father Duffy Square), Manhattan, New York; galleries, museums, theaters nationwide
cases.description: Cuban artist and activist Tania Bruguera staged her landmark participatory performance "Tatlin's Whisper #6 (Havana Version)" (2009, on loan from the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum) in Times Square on May 1, 2026 (International Workers' Day/May Day), in partnership with "Fall of Freedom." The performance — a microphone, a raised platform, and one minute of uncensored speech per participant — originated at the 2009 Havana Biennial as a platform for free speech denied under Cuban authoritarianism. Its staging in Times Square on May Day 2026 explicitly frames current US governance as analogous: "I think it's important to create connections between situations that apparently have nothing to do with each other, for example, repression in Cuba and what is happening in the United States," Bruguera told Hyperallergic. Fall of Freedom is a new national arts resistance platform launched May 1, 2026, calling on galleries, museums, libraries, comedy clubs, theaters, and concert halls across the country to host exhibitions and performances defying "authoritarian forces sweeping the nation." Times Square Arts Director Anna Starling: "We are honored to bring Tatlin's Whisper #6 back to the Crossroads of the World, this time on May Day, to open up a temporary public forum where speech itself becomes the artwork." Bruguera has been repeatedly detained by Cuban authorities for her artistic and civic work.
cases.outcome: Performance completed May 1. Fall of Freedom platform launched, ongoing.
cases.tags: Political art, Protest art, Resistance, Censorship
cases.notes: The "thermometer" framing from Bruguera's own theoretical vocabulary is exactly the tracker's thermometer function applied by the artist herself — the performance "doesn't turn out well or badly; it simply turns out. What exists is what will be seen." The Cuba-US analogy is delicate but deliberate: Bruguera isn't equating the regimes, but connecting the mechanism (silence normalized as a precondition for stability). Hannah Arendt's framing she cites: authoritarianism and totalitarianism don't belong to one ideological camp. Fall of Freedom as a platform is worth tracking — it positions itself as a structural arts-sector response to the federal censorship cluster (034/011/012/051/049), and its decentralized open-invitation format is distinct from specific artist actions. Connects to the Wende Museum / Pepperdine case (049): institutions specializing in documenting authoritarian censorship of art are themselves becoming the venues for censored work. Bruguera's "arte de conducta" framework — art as civic conduct — is pedagogically useful for ARTH 201. GOVERNANCE NOTE: Democracy with significant authoritarian tendencies.
cases.interested_parties: Tania Bruguera (artist); Times Square Arts / Anna Starling (Director); Fall of Freedom (platform); Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum (work on loan); galleries, museums, theaters nationwide (Fall of Freedom participants)

cases.title: Loi-cadre sur la restitution des biens culturels spoliés durant la colonisation — definitively adopted
cases.institution: Assemblée nationale / Sénat, Paris
cases.description: RESOLUTION: The French repatriation framework law was definitively adopted by both chambers of parliament. Sequence: (1) The CMP (commission mixte paritaire) produced a unified compromise text on April 30, reconciling the Assemblée nationale's April 13 amended text with the Senate's January 2026 version. (2) The National Assembly voted unanimously 141-0 on Wednesday May 6. (3) The Senate voted unanimously on Thursday May 7. Culture Minister Catherine Pégard declared: "L'instant est historique." The law now awaits formal promulgation by President Macron (15-day constitutional clock from May 7 = approximately by May 22). The law enables restitutions by government decree without requiring individual parliamentary votes, covering cultural property acquired between 1815 and 1972. Two scientific and parliamentary commissions must consult on each case. Pending requests from Algeria, Mali, Benin, Chad, Ethiopia, Ivory Coast, Madagascar, Ghana, Senegal now have a legal pathway once promulgated. Approximately 150,000 African objects held in ~230 French public museums. Separately: a bill for repatriation of Kali'na human remains from Guyana is expected before the Senate on May 18.
cases.outcome: Both chambers adopted unanimously. Awaiting Macron promulgation by approximately May 22. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING: Macron signature; Kali'na bill Senate May 18; first restitution requests under new framework]
cases.tags: Repatriation, Colonial legacy, Legislative action, Ethical museum
cases.notes: Major resolution of this long-running [FOLLOW-UP PENDING] case. The CMP conditionality debate (RN's "bonne conservation" amendment vs. left's desire for broader scope) was resolved in the final compromise text. The African Futures Lab critique remains the decolonial counter-narrative — the law enables restitution without naming colonialism. The simultaneity with Venice Biennale opening week is a useful juxtaposition: Europe's cultural institutions simultaneously opening to geopolitical controversy and legislatively beginning to address their own colonial collections. The Kali'na bill (for Guyanese Indigenous human remains in Paris) pending May 18 adds an Overseas France dimension not covered by the main law. Once Macron signs, the specific pending claims become active legal processes. Senatorial centrist Catherine Morin-Desailly: the parliament "opens a way where memory is shared, not confiscated, where history's wounds become foundations for renewed dialogue." The word 'colonialism' remains absent from the text.
cases.interested_parties: Macron (promulgation pending); Catherine Pégard (Culture Minister); Assemblée nationale (141-0, May 6); Sénat (unanimous, May 7); CMP (unified text April 30); Algeria/Mali/Benin/Chad/Ethiopia/Ivory Coast/Madagascar/Ghana/Senegal (requesting states); African Futures Lab (critic)

cases.title: Post-Orbán de-politicization of Hungarian cultural institutions — Magyar sworn in as PM
cases.institution: Hungarian Parliament (neo-Gothic building, Budapest); Kossuth Square (celebration)
cases.description: UPDATE: Péter Magyar took his oath of office on May 9, 2026, becoming Hungary's new prime minister and ending 16 years of Orbán's autocratic rule. Tisza holds 141 of 199 parliamentary seats — the largest vote share of any post-Communist Hungarian party ever. In his parliamentary speech, Magyar explicitly called on Fidesz-appointed heads of government institutions, including President Tamás Sulyok, to resign no later than May 31. Magyar plans to form a National Asset Recovery and Protection Office to investigate misuse of public funds under Orbán. He also stated the government will suspend public broadcaster news programming until objectivity is restored. Symbolically: the EU flag was raised on the Parliament building's façade for the first time since 2014, when Orbán's government removed it. Tens of thousands celebrated in Kossuth Square. Cabinet includes Zoltán Tarr (culture minister) and Andrea Rost (opera singer, government commissioner for music culture). The May 9 swearing-in coincided exactly with the Venice Biennale's public opening.
cases.outcome: Magyar sworn in May 9. May 31 voluntary resignation deadline for Orbán-era institution heads now active and counting. Cabinet formation complete. EU flag raised on Parliament.
cases.tags: Political interference, Institutional crisis, Funding dispute, Self-censorship
cases.notes: The EU flag moment is the cultural shorthand for the whole transition: a symbolic assertion of European democratic values that Orbán had literally removed from the building. The May 31 deadline is now live — 22 days for Júlia Fabényi (Ludwig Museum) and MMA leadership to step aside voluntarily. The coincidence with Venice Biennale public opening on May 9 is worth noting for class: the day Europe's most contested art exhibition opened to the public, Hungary formally installed a government committed to reversing arts-sector capture. These are two faces of the same European cultural governance moment. GOVERNANCE NOTE: Hungary transitioning from illiberal capture toward democratic norms — May 31 is the first hard institutional accountability date.
cases.interested_parties: Péter Magyar / Tisza (PM, sworn in May 9); President Tamás Sulyok (called to resign by May 31); Zoltán Tarr (culture minister-designate); Andrea Rost (opera singer / music commissioner); Júlia Fabényi (Ludwig Museum, under May 31 deadline); Hungarian Academy of Arts (MMA, restructuring pending); EU Commission (€17B frozen funds being unlocked)

cases.title: Eisenhower Executive Office Building — NCPC hearing outcome, May 7
cases.institution: Eisenhower Executive Office Building, Washington DC; National Capital Planning Commission
cases.description: The National Capital Planning Commission held a 1.5-hour hearing May 7 on Trump's proposal to paint the EEOB's granite exterior white at an estimated cost of $7.5M+. The NCPC unanimously approved cleaning the exterior but declined to approve the painting proposal, instead requesting additional information: how the silicate paint would affect the historic granite, ongoing maintenance costs, and whether less intrusive alternatives (such as exterior lighting) could achieve the desired 'brightening' without painting. Preservationists and public commenters had filed more than 2,000 comments opposing the paint. A federal lawsuit challenging the proposed paint job is already pending. The NCPC is chaired by Will Scharf, a senior Trump White House aide — a conflict of interest flagged in entry 050 (White House ballroom). Commission's decision to request more information rather than approve or deny leaves the project in procedural limbo; a future NCPC hearing will address the paint proposal.
cases.outcome: NCPC approved cleaning only; declined to approve painting; requested additional information. Future hearing required. Lawsuit pending.
cases.tags: Architectural preservation, Design controversy, Landmark dispute, Legal challenge
cases.notes: The NCPC's caution — even with Trump-aligned commission members — suggests the granite-paint proposal faces substantive scientific and legal obstacles. The preservationists' core argument (granite is not designed for paint; silicate paint traps moisture; damage would be irreversible to an 1888 landmark) carried weight with commissioners. The conflict of interest (Scharf chairing the body reviewing his employer's proposal) parallels entry 050's White House ballroom NCPC issue. The 'additional information' request delays but does not block the project. Watch for next NCPC hearing date, CFA decision, and court ruling. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING]
cases.interested_parties: National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC; chair Will Scharf, Trump White House aide); Trump administration / White House Office of Administration (Ryan Erb, facilities); preservationists; architects; historians; 2,000+ public commenters (opposed); federal court (pending lawsuit)

cases.title: National Endowment for the Humanities — DOGE grant terminations ruled unconstitutional
cases.artist: Multiple grantees (scholars, writers, research institutions nationwide)
cases.institution: National Endowment for the Humanities / US District Court, Southern District of New York
cases.description: DOGE used ChatGPT to identify and terminate over 1,400 NEH grants totaling $100M+, targeting any grant the AI flagged as DEI-related, without defining DEI for the chatbot before using its outputs. Grants canceled included Holocaust education programming at Seton Hall University, a virtual reality demonstration of Indigenous culture at Mesa Verde and Wupatki National Monuments, and a book about HIV in prisons. ChatGPT incorrectly flagged as DEI an anthology titled 'In the Shadow of the Holocaust: Short Fiction by Jewish Writers from the Soviet Union.' On May 7, 2026, US District Judge Colleen McMahon (SDNY) permanently barred the administration from terminating the grants, ruling DOGE violated the First Amendment and the Fifth Amendment's equal protection clause, and had no statutory authority. 'DOGE had no statutory authority to terminate NEH grants,' McMahon wrote. She called the case 'a textbook example of unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination.' The court rejected the government's argument that ChatGPT's misclassifications absolved it of constitutional responsibility: 'ChatGPT was the Government's chosen instrument for purposes of this project, and DOGE's use of AI to identify DEI-related material neither excuses presumptively unconstitutional conduct nor gives the Government carte blanche to engage in it.' Government ordered to rescind termination letters; not immediately required to pay grant funds (only the Court of Federal Claims can compel payment). Appeal not confirmed as of May 9. Case brought by Authors Guild, American Council of Learned Societies, American Historical Association, Modern Language Association, and individual grantees.
cases.outcome: Judge permanently barred grant terminations May 7, 2026. Government ordered to rescind termination letters. Appeal not confirmed. Ruling does not immediately compel payment.
cases.tags: Censorship, Political interference, Funding dispute, Legal challenge
cases.notes: Analytically the richest DOGE/arts entry in the tracker. The ChatGPT-as-censor mechanism is genuinely new: algorithmic viewpoint discrimination in which the AI inferred what its users wanted to find and supplied rationales accordingly — McMahon's hypothesis is that the AI was 'guessing at what reviewers wanted to find in order to flag grants ripe for termination.' The misclassification of a Holocaust/Soviet Jewish anthology as DEI is the sharpest illustration: the mechanism's absurdity is also evidence of AI hallucination the judge explicitly flagged. The court's rejection of the 'it was ChatGPT's fault' defense is important precedent for AI-assisted governance decisions generally. The affected grants — Holocaust education, Indigenous VR, HIV-in-prisons book — illustrate the breadth of cultural programming erased. Distinct from entry 034 (NEA grant cancellations, which covers the National Endowment for the Arts and ongoing elimination efforts). NEA and NEH are separate agencies; this case is NEH-specific. Connects to entries 012 (Smithsonian), 007 (Philadelphia slavery exhibit), 005 (Kennedy Center) as the federal cultural suppression pattern. McMahon's phrase 'textbook example of unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination' is the teaching anchor. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING: government appeal expected; watch for filing and outcome]
cases.interested_parties: DOGE (Justin Fox, Nate Cavanaugh — both tech-sector recruits); NEH acting chair Michael McDonald; Judge Colleen McMahon (SDNY); Authors Guild; American Council of Learned Societies; American Historical Association; Modern Language Association of America; individual grantees

cases.title: Vaillancourt Fountain — demolition and accidental fire
cases.institution: Justin Herman Plaza, San Francisco, California
cases.description: Demolition of the 1971 Brutalist Vaillancourt Fountain began May 4 after the California appeals court denied a final injunction request from the preservation coalition Friends of the Plaza. On May 6, construction crews accidentally ignited debris inside the fountain's cantilevered steel tubes during torch-cutting; a San Francisco Arts Commission spokesperson confirmed the fire was controlled with continuous water spraying, with no major damage. Demolition is continuing. The city's rationale centered on asbestos contamination; the Friends of the Plaza alleged asbestos was pretextual — the city wanted to remove an aesthetically unpopular work without engaging the preservation question on its merits. The fountain, commissioned by the San Francisco Arts Commission in 1969 and completed in 1971, was one of the largest public art installations on the West Coast. The preservation fight lasted years.
cases.outcome: Demolition underway as of May 8. Court denied preservation injunction. Work continuing.
cases.tags: Demolition, Architectural preservation, Legal challenge, Public art
cases.notes: Brutalist public sculpture is undertracked in this database — Vaillancourt's fountain is one of the most contentious public sculptures in US history, defended on principle by preservationists despite near-universal aesthetic dismissal. The 'safety' rationale (asbestos) is contested as pretextual — the city's willingness to absorb litigation costs suggests the goal was removal regardless of legal vehicle. The accidental fire during demolition adds a mordant coda to a decades-long civic argument about aesthetic authority. Theme 6 (When is iconoclasm justified?) applied to democratic processes: court-approved removal, not mob action. Enrich Friday West Coast trawl with local coverage. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING: completion of demolition; any subsequent legal or civic response]
cases.interested_parties: Armand Vaillancourt (artist); Friends of the Plaza (preservation coalition, lost appeals court injunction); San Francisco Arts Commission; California appeals court; City of San Francisco

cases.title: 2026 Venice Biennale — public opening day; mass artist withdrawal from Visitor Lions; ANGA strike aftermath
cases.artist: 54 artists in 'In Minor Keys'; 16 national pavilion teams; ANGA
cases.institution: La Biennale di Venezia, Venice
cases.description: On public opening day (May 9), 54 of 111 artists in the main exhibition 'In Minor Keys' and 16 national pavilion teams formally withdrew from Visitor Lions consideration via an e-flux statement, in solidarity with the resigned jury and protesting the inclusion of Israel and Russia. Withdrawing pavilions include Belgium, France, Luxembourg, Spain, Netherlands, Poland, Slovenia, Lithuania, Latvia, Switzerland, Ecuador, Ireland, and others. The withdrawal follows yesterday's historic 24-hour labor strike (May 8) in which at least 27 pavilions closed partially or fully, the Arsenale was shuttered, and thousands marched on Via Garibaldi. Police used batons and shields against protesters attempting to enter the Arsenale, where Israel's temporary pavilion is located. Gabrielle Goliath (South Africa, entry 006) marched in the strike, confirming her independent exhibition opened at the Chiesa di Sant'Antonin in Castello, where it runs May 5–July 31. Hyperallergic's Hakim Bishara described yesterday's march as the first cultural strike in the Biennale's 131-year history. Almost half of the Biennale's international exhibition participants have now collectively refused the award system the Foundation created to replace the resigned jury's Golden Lions.
cases.outcome: Withdrawal announced May 9. Historic strike completed May 8. Visitor Lions to be voted by public; results November 22, 2026. All contested pavilions still open. EU May 11 funding deadline still running.
cases.tags: Geopolitics, Protest, Boycott, Institutional risk, Labor dispute
cases.notes: The withdrawal from the Visitor Lions completes the institutional collapse that began with the jury resignation (008-I). The Foundation's pivot to public voting was intended to depoliticize the awards; almost half the participants refusing to enter re-politicizes it on day one of public access. The Gaza-born artist Mohammed Joha, whose mother and sister were killed in Israeli airstrikes, marching in the strike and included in the main exhibition while the Israeli state exhibits meters away in the Arsenale, is the human distillation of the entire controversy. The police beating of protesters at the Arsenale entrance is itself a story about the state's relationship to cultural space. France's own pavilion representative (Yto Barrada) withdrawing from a French-state-sponsored award competition is analytically notable. Visitor Lions results November 22 — six months of live controversy remain. Cross-reference 008-I (jury resigned), 008-N/P (strike announced/held), 006-B (Goliath at Sant'Antonin), 016 (Cesar Chavez — note different entry 016 from session error; Venice parent is entry 008). Alfredo Jaar, Zoe Leonard, Walid Raad, Cauleen Smith, Otobong Nkanga, Carolina Caycedo, Florence Lazar, Joana Hadjithomas & Khalil Joreige, Mohammed Joha, Vera Tamari, Avi Mograbi & Avital Barak, Tuan Andrew Nguyen, Hala Schoukair, Berni Searle, Yoshiko Shimada, and others; national pavilion teams including Belgium (Miet Warlop), France (Yto Barrada), Spain (Oriol Vilanova), Netherlands (Dries Verhoeven), Poland, Switzerland, Luxembourg, Slovenia, Lithuania, Latvia, Ecuador, Ireland; ANGA; Art Not Genocide Alliance; Sale Docks; Mi Riconosci?; Biennalocene; 3 Italian unions; Gabrielle Goliath (SA, marching)

cases.title: Eisenhower Executive Office Building (EEOB) exterior — proposed painting
cases.institution: Eisenhower Executive Office Building, 17th Street & Pennsylvania Avenue NW, Washington DC
cases.description: President Trump is pursuing the painting of the entire granite exterior of the Eisenhower Executive Office Building (EEOB) — a National Historic Landmark and National Register of Historic Places site completed in 1888 — bright white. Trump stated the current gray granite is 'a really bad color.' The White House Office of Administration proposed two options: painting the entire exterior, or painting most of it while leaving the granite base unpainted (the full paint is preferred). Estimated cost: at least $7.5 million, per White House facilities official Ryan Erb at a May 7 NCPC hearing. Preservationists, architects, and historians have raised alarms that granite is not designed to receive paint and that silicate paint would trap moisture, accelerating stone deterioration — potentially irreversible damage to an 1888 landmark. More than 2,000 public comments submitted to the NCPC were strongly opposed. The Commission of Fine Arts (Trump-appointed) directed White House to present more information at a future date at an earlier hearing; at the May 7 NCPC hearing, commissioners unanimously approved cleaning the building's exterior but declined to approve the paint proposal, instead requesting additional information including a third-party assessment of the granite's condition and details on the proposed silicate paint. A federal lawsuit against the proposed paint job is already working its way through court. The NCPC is chaired by Will Scharf, a Trump White House aide — the same conflict-of-interest pattern flagged in entry 050 (White House ballroom: NCPC chair simultaneously serving the project's patron).
cases.outcome: NCPC review May 7: approved cleaning, declined to approve painting, requested additional information. CFA previously directed more information. Federal lawsuit pending. No painting approved as of May 8. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING: NCPC future hearing; CFA decision; court ruling]
cases.tags: Architectural preservation, Design controversy, Landmark dispute, Legal challenge, Funding dispute, Political interference
cases.notes: [FOLLOW-UP PENDING] Fifth entry in the DC monumental core cluster alongside 038/038-A (triumphal arch), 046 (Reflecting Pool), 050/050-A/050-B (White House ballroom), 063 (National Garden of Heroes). The EEOB case has a distinct character from the others: this is not a new construction but a proposed irreversible alteration of a National Historic Landmark's original material fabric. The experts' core argument — granite cannot be safely painted, trapped moisture will deteriorate the stone — means approval could cause permanent damage to an 1888 building that survived intact for 138 years. The 'magic paint with silicate' framing from Trump's private advocacy (per CNN) puts the president in the role of amateur materials scientist, with preservation professionals uniformly opposed. The cost trajectory ($7.5M preliminary estimate, no ceiling announced) follows the same scope-inflation pattern as the triumphal arch (38: $60ft → 250ft) and White House ballroom (050: $200M → $551M). The NCPC chair conflict-of-interest is the governance pattern: Will Scharf serves simultaneously as a senior White House staffer and as chair of the commission reviewing White House-sponsored projects. The 2,000+ public comments opposed to painting — and the commission's declining to approve — partially check the project, but the CFA approval track record (38-A: approved triumphal arch concept over 99% opposition) sets a cautionary precedent for what Trump-appointed commissions do when pushed. The 1888 completion date is worth noting for class: the EEOB was designed and built during the Gilded Age, during which the Second Empire style was already falling from fashion — it's been considered aesthetically problematic almost from the day it opened. Trump's 'bad color' critique is thus not historically novel. What is novel is a proposal to paint the granite, which no prior administration ever contemplated. GOVERNANCE NOTE: Democracy with significant authoritarian tendencies. Executive action on cultural institutions exceeds normal democratic norms: ideological conditions attached to public funding, bypass of established review processes (Section 106, NCPC, CFA), contempt for or circumvention of court orders, and use of federal funding as a coercive instrument.

cases.title: Die große Nacht im Eimer (The Big Night Down the Drain, 1962–63) / Der nackte Mann (The Naked Man, 1962)
cases.institution: Galerie Werner & Katz, West Berlin, West Germany
cases.description: RETROSPECTIVE ENTRY, occasioned by Baselitz's death April 30, 2026. At his first solo exhibition in October 1963 at Galerie Werner & Katz in West Berlin, two paintings were seized by the public prosecutor's office two days after opening on grounds of 'infringement of public morality' (Unsittlichkeit): Die große Nacht im Eimer (depicting a distorted figure with an exaggerated phallus, widely read as a Hitler-like figure masturbating) and Der nackte Mann (a nude youth gripping a monstrous phallus). A friend of gallerist Michael Werner had reportedly already tipped off the German News Agency's local paper B.Z. — making the seizure partly a self-fulfilling, intentional scandal. Baselitz was charged with offending public morality. Criminal proceedings lasted until October 1965, when the case was dismissed and the paintings returned. The episode made Baselitz famous and effectively launched his career in the West. His stated intention was to provoke a reckoning with post-war German amnesia: 'I proceed from a state of disharmony, from ugly things.' Both paintings are now held at Museum Ludwig, Cologne. Die große Nacht im Eimer is widely considered one of the landmark works of postwar European art.
cases.outcome: Resolved 1965: criminal case dismissed, paintings returned. Both now at Museum Ludwig, Cologne.
cases.tags: Censorship, Obscenity, Legal challenge, Political art
cases.notes: Retrospective entry added to the tracker, occasioned by Baselitz's death at 88 on April 30, 2026. Analytically this is a clean Theme 1 case operating in a specific governance context: post-war West German democracy attempting to re-establish cultural norms after Nazism, producing obscenity prosecution of exactly the kind of raw, ugly, body-centered painting that Baselitz argued was necessary to confront what Nazism and the war had done. The irony is structural — the democratic state prosecutes the work that is trying to look at what the fascist state did. The seizure's premeditated quality (Werner's friend tipping the press before the prosecutor acted) is analytically interesting: Baselitz and Werner may have engineered the scandal, making the state's censorship apparatus a collaborator in the career launch. The paintings' current resting place at Museum Ludwig is itself a statement — now canonical, exhibited in a major public institution, the very works that were seized as obscene. Thermometer function: the controversy is fully resolved and the cultural context has shifted to the point where 'Die große Nacht im Eimer' is a curriculum staple. Compare the trajectory to Piss Christ (entry 045-A traces the Serrano arc) and the Marc Quinn blood works logic: cultural noise eventually recedes, content becomes legible. Additional controversy cluster: Baselitz's 1980 Venice Biennale sculpture (wooden figure widely read as Nazi salute, which he denied), logged separately if you want a second retrospective entry. His repeated statements that women 'don't paint very well' also constitute a documented pattern of institutional sexism from an art-world titan — connects to ARTH 201 Theme 8 (artist responsibility to audiences).
cases.interested_parties: Georg Baselitz (artist); Michael Werner (gallerist); West Berlin public prosecutor's office; B.Z. newspaper; Museum Ludwig, Cologne (current holder)

cases.title: American Folk Art Museum labor dispute

cases.institution: American Folk Art Museum, New York City; Mandarin Oriental, Columbus Circle (picket site)
cases.description: Workers at the American Folk Art Museum picketed the museum's annual gala at the Mandarin Oriental hotel in Columbus Circle on May 6, joined by UAW Local 2110 organizers. Approximately 36 union members and supporters marched for two hours, holding signs reading 'For Folk's Sake' and 'Self Taught, Not Self Funded,' chanting against poverty wages and union busting. Workers have been negotiating a new contract since shortly after voting to join UAW Local 2110 in June 2024 — nearly two years of stalled negotiations. Frontline workers (visitor services, gift shop, building maintenance) earn $19/hour or $58,686/year, approximately $12,000 below MIT's calculated living wage for NYC. Management offered $21.50/hour max by year three; union demanded $30/hour by year three, plus health care and hybrid schedule guarantees. CEO Jason Busch's compensation in FY2024 was $321,882 per tax filings.
cases.outcome: Negotiations stalled. Gala picketed May 6. No contract reached as of May 8. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING]

The 'For Folk's Sake' / 'Self Taught, Not Self Funded' sign wordplay captures the irony: a museum celebrating the labor of self-taught artists whose workers cannot afford to live in the city where they work. cases.title: US museum building repairs crisis (GAO-26-108485 report)
cases.institution: Museums nationwide — approximately 16,700 public and private nonprofit museums, 50 states and DC
cases.description: A March 2026 Government Accountability Office report (GAO-26-108485), covered today by The Art Newspaper and ARTnews, documents a systemic crisis in US museum infrastructure. Key findings from a survey of approximately 300 museums and 17 site visits: (1) About 85% of museums (13,700) have a backlog of deferred maintenance and repair needs. (2) About 77% (12,300) have at least one building system in poor condition putting collections at risk. (3) About 73% (11,900) cite at least one health or safety concern. (4) Nearly half have physical accessibility barriers. (5) About half report more than $100,000 in deferred maintenance each. (6) Only 11% expect the backlog to shrink in three years. Root cause: federal IMLS funding legally may not be used for construction or capital improvements — only programs and services. Museums rely primarily on private donations for structural needs. Rural and tribal museums face compounding challenges. The report provides Congress with data as it considers IMLS reauthorization, which lapsed in 2025. Trump's FY2027 budget proposes eliminating IMLS; Congress has continued funding at $291.8M for FY2026. Example cited in report: a small museum in Alaska with a $212,000 annual budget needing $289,000 in building repairs. Federal museums excluded from scope.
cases.outcome: GAO report published March 2026. Covered today. No federal legislative response yet. IMLS authorization lapsed; Trump budget proposes elimination.
cases.tags: Funding dispute, Institutional crisis, Conservation
cases.notes: Structural context entry. The Kennedy Center's water damage toured for media (005-C) and the GSA buildings with New Deal murals (040) are downstream manifestations of the same infrastructure neglect the GAO documents system-wide. The tribal museum dimension connects to 019 (THPO elimination) and 068 (Las Playas Intaglio) — federal preservation infrastructure defunded while physical collections are simultaneously made more vulnerable. The accessibility finding connects to the public access themes across the tracker. The irony that Trump proposes eliminating IMLS while bypassing federal review processes that protect historic buildings (Kennedy Center, White House ballroom) illuminates the full pattern: cultural infrastructure under pressure from multiple directions simultaneously. Connects to Theme 2 at scale — what does it mean that 85% of the nation's museums cannot maintain the buildings that hold their collections?
cases.interested_parties: US Government Accountability Office (GAO); David Marroni (GAO contact); Institute of Museum and Library Services (IMLS); Association of Tribal Archives, Libraries and Museums / Susan Feller; museum staff nationwide; Congress

cases.title: America250 vs. Freedom250 rivalry; 'History Rocks!' cancellations; 'Rededicate 250' National Mall event
cases.institution: National Mall, Washington DC; schools nationwide; 250.gov
cases.description: Two organizations compete to shape the US 250th anniversary (July 4, 2026). America250 is the bipartisan congressional commission established in 2016 (co-chaired by Bush and Obama, 350-member Congressional caucus). Freedom250 is a Trump-aligned public-private partnership launched December 2025, operating through 250.gov with fewer public reporting requirements. Congress appropriated $150M to the Department of Interior; most is now expected redirected to Freedom250. The IMLS originally awarded America250 a $10M grant for six Freedom Truck mobile exhibitions; this was redirected to Freedom250 in December, with exhibits now organized by PragerU and Hillsdale College, presenting American history without reference to slavery or Indigenous genocide. Education Secretary Linda McMahon's 'History Rocks!' school tour — billed as nonpartisan — has been canceled at 4+ locations (Massachusetts, Alabama, two in Connecticut) and met with protests at others (Wisconsin, New Jersey, Illinois). Cancellations are driven by the tour's exclusive sponsorship by the America 250 Civics Education Coalition, composed entirely of conservative and religious organizations (Turning Point USA, Moms for Liberty, Heritage Foundation, America First Policy Institute). 'Rededicate 250' event planned for National Mall on May 17 includes far-right Christian nationalist speakers; White House described it as a 'large-scale revival.' Freedom250 events include a UFC fight on the White House Ellipse (June 14) and an IndyCar race on the National Mall. Corporate sponsors including Mastercard, SAP, Deloitte, and Lockheed Martin are listed for Freedom250. Congress has appropriated a total of $150M; America250 has received ~$25M, Freedom250 ~$22M; final allocation unresolved.
cases.outcome: Both programs operating in parallel. Freedom250 controls increasing share of federal funding. 'History Rocks!' cancellations continuing. 'Rededicate 250' National Mall event scheduled May 17. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING: May 17 event; further History Rocks! cancellations; congressional oversight]

cases.title: Las Playas Intaglio (c. 1000 CE)
cases.institution: Cabeza Prieta National Wildlife Refuge, Southwest Arizona (US-Mexico border)
cases.description: On April 23, 2026, a contractor building Trump's 'Smart Wall' border reinforcement ran heavy construction equipment through the Las Playas Intaglio, a 272-foot-long fish-shaped geoglyph etched into the desert pavement of Cabeza Prieta National Wildlife Refuge in Southwest Arizona. Approximately 60–70 feet of the intaglio were damaged. The intaglio is estimated to be at least 1,000 years old and is a sacred site for ancestors of the Tohono O'odham Nation, which lies east of the refuge. CBP confirmed the damage on May 1, describing it as 'inadvertent,' and stated that CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott was 'engaged directly with tribal leadership to determine appropriate next steps.' The remaining portion of the site was secured. The intaglio's existence and cultural significance had been extensively documented, including in US Supreme Court amicus filings during Trump's first term. Preservation archaeologist Aaron Wright, who visited the site in April out of concern about Smart Wall construction and filmed it days before the damage, told Hyperallergic: 'It's a grim reality that the nation's heritage basically dangles on the whim of an administration. We have these environmental laws in place, but then we have other laws that basically nullify them at the will of the executive.' Trump's border emergency declaration superseded standard environmental review processes under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). During Trump's first term, contractors also damaged a Hohokam burial ground in the same region. Smart Wall construction also threatens Quitobaquito Springs in Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument. Florida Governor DeSantis similarly invoked emergency orders to build the 'Alligator Alcatraz' prison on sacred Miccosukee land.
cases.outcome: 60-70 feet of 272-foot intaglio damaged April 23. CBP confirmed damage May 1. Remaining site secured. Tribal leadership consultation underway. No restoration announced.
cases.tags: Vandalism, Conservation, Indigenous rights, Historical erasure, Political interference
cases.notes: [FOLLOW-UP PENDING] This is a distinct category from the tracker's other heritage destruction entries. Entries 037 (Iran war) and 047 (Sudan museums) document wartime collateral destruction; this is active federal infrastructure construction damaging a documented sacred site in peacetime on US soil — made possible by the executive's self-granted authority to waive environmental protection laws via emergency declaration. The NEPA waiver mechanism is the governance story: Wright's framing ('other laws basically nullify them at the will of the executive') describes a structural condition, not an accident. The fact that the intaglio's existence and sacred status were recorded in Supreme Court filings during Trump's first term makes the 'inadvertent' framing legally and morally strained — it was known, documented, and damaged anyway. The pattern within Trump's border construction is now a documented sequence: Hohokam burial ground (first term), Las Playas Intaglio (second term), Quitobaquito Springs (threatened). Connects structurally to entry 019 (THPO funding elimination, which defunds the very preservation infrastructure that would flag such sites for protection) — the defunding of tribal historic preservation officers and the waiver of NEPA create compounding vulnerability. The 'Smart Wall' multi-billion-dollar project is the current construction vehicle. Coverage geography: Washington Post broke the story nationally; Hyperallergic is the arts-sector pickup. Enrich with Indigenous press sources next Saturday (Middle East/non-Francophone Africa/South Asia trawl day covers Indigenous-adjacent cases). Watch for Tohono O'odham Nation formal response and any congressional or legal challenge to the CBP contractor. GOVERNANCE NOTE: Democracy with significant authoritarian tendencies. The executive's use of emergency declarations to waive statutory environmental protections — including those specifically designed to protect Native American sacred sites — is a structural governance failure consistent with the broader pattern documented across entries 005, 007, 019, 034, 038, 046, and 050.
cases.interested_parties: CBP / Commissioner Rodney Scott; Trump administration (border emergency declaration); CBP contractor (unnamed); Tohono O'odham Nation; Aaron Wright (preservation archaeologist, Arizona); Washington Post (broke story April 30); Hyperallergic (follow-up reporting)

cases.title: Tlali (2026)
cases.institution: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA), Geffen Plaza, Los Angeles CA
cases.description: Mexican artist Pedro Reyes unveiled Tlali (2026), a four-metre-tall Olmec-inspired volcanic-stone sculpture of a female face, installed on the exterior of the new David Geffen Galleries building at LACMA as a permanent commission. An open letter signed by nearly 80 Mexican cultural figures, published April 23 in the Spanish-language criticism site Cubo Blanco, alleges the work is a revised version of a commission Reyes received in 2021 to replace Mexico City's 1877 Columbus statue on the Paseo de la Reforma — a project that was canceled after objections from more than 300 cultural figures and collectives. The objections in 2021 centered on: (1) Reyes is a male, non-Indigenous artist commissioned to represent 'the Indigenous woman'; (2) the work 'reproduces the silencing and invisibilisation of women's struggles and their Indigenous communities'; (3) it exhibits 'neo-indigenist overtones' and a 'vagueness typical of 19th-century national statuary.' The 2023 letter objects to the LACMA commission on the same grounds, and adds: the title was shortened from 'Tlalli' (Nahuatl for Earth) to 'Tlali' to 'appeal to anglophones'; a Nahuatl word is used for an Olmec-inspired work (a different culture); and the original Mexico City site was ultimately transformed into the Glorieta de las Mujeres que Luchan (Roundabout of the Women Who Fight), a feminist anti-monument against gender violence and femicide, making the export of the rejected sculpture to a US museum feel like a disrespect to that struggle. LACMA describes the work as 'entirely different in purpose and meaning' from the 2021 Mexico City proposal, noting the face's features were reshaped and the commission offers 'a new location, context and opportunity for discussion.' LACMA director Michael Govan said the visible armature was central to discussions with the artist: 'Museums are a kind of armature for history.' Reyes did not respond to press requests.
cases.outcome: Sculpture installed permanently at LACMA. Open letter published April 23 with ~80 signatories. No removal demanded. No LACMA retraction. LACMA defending commission.
cases.tags: Community objection, Racial/ethnic sensitivity, Indigenous rights, Authenticity, Design controversy
cases.notes: [FOLLOW-UP PENDING] This case is analytically dense. Several distinct threads: (1) The 'recycled rejection' problem — LACMA acquired a commission that was rejected in its country of origin, without appearing to reckon with why it was rejected. María Minera's framing is sharp: 'this commission is the same one denounced in Mexico for Indigenous stereotypes and perpetuating colonialism.' The institutional question for Theme 5: does an encyclopedic museum have an obligation to investigate the controversy history of a commissioned work before installing it permanently? (2) The representational standing question: a non-Indigenous male artist commissioned to represent Indigenous women — the 2021 objection stands unchanged at LACMA. (3) The Nahuatl/Olmec mismatch: using a Nahuatl word for an Olmec-inspired work conflates two distinct pre-Columbian cultures, which critics read as neo-indigenist flattening of Indigenous specificity. (4) The Glorieta dimension: the original site has become a living feminist memorial against femicide; exporting the rejected sculpture to a high-profile US museum retroactively rehabilitates it in a way that feels disrespectful to the women who transformed that space. (5) The titling decision ('Tlali' vs. 'Tlalli') for Anglophone consumption — a small change that carries large symbolic weight about whose reception is being prioritized. LACMA's 'armature' framing is interesting but sidesteps the political history. Compare entry 014 (AztLÁn exhibition at Bellas Artes, Mexico City) as a counterpoint: Mexican cultural institutions hosting work that responds to Indigenous/Chicano erasure, while a US institution acquires a work rejected in Mexico for Indigenous stereotyping. The coverage geography is notable — this is primarily a story in Mexican cultural press (Cubo Blanco) picked up by The Art Newspaper; it has not received wide US arts press attention yet. Enrich next Friday (West Coast US trawl) and next Monday (Latin America trawl) with Spanish-language sources.

cases.title: White House State Ballroom / East Wing — Senate Republicans insert $1B security funding into immigration bill
cases.institution: US Senate; White House East Wing site, Washington DC
cases.description: UPDATE: Senate Republicans inserted $1 billion for White House East Wing 'security enhancements' into a roughly $70 billion immigration enforcement funding bill released May 5. The provision was added by the Senate Judiciary Committee (Chair: Sen. Charles Grassley). The bill does not mention the ballroom explicitly, but the money is directed to 'security adjustments and upgrades, including within the perimeter fence of the White House compound to support enhancements by the Secret Service relating to the East Wing Modernization Project, including above-ground and below-ground security features.' A bar on spending for 'non-security elements' is included. Trump had previously insisted the renovation would be funded by private donations. White House spokesman Davis Ingle praised the security funding. After the April 25 WHCD shooting (see 050-A), some congressional Republicans proposed $400M in direct federal funding for the ballroom; Democrats blocked that. The $1B immigration-bill provision is a second attempt, packaged with immigration enforcement funding to use the filibuster-proof reconciliation process. If enacted, it could clear the legal obstacles Judge Leon identified — he ruled the project required congressional approval. Democrats signaled immediate opposition: Sen. Schumer called it 'a Trump ballroom.' Sen. Brian Schatz noted all senators would get 'an up or down vote on the ballroom.' Democrats plan to use it as a 2026 midterm election issue.
cases.outcome: Senate provision released May 5. Bill advancing via reconciliation. Judge Leon injunction still in effect. Democrats opposing. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING: Senate vote timeline; whether $1B provision survives; whether enactment clears Judge Leon's injunction.]
cases.tags: Funding dispute, Legal challenge, Political interference, Design controversy
cases.notes: [FOLLOW-UP PENDING] This is the most significant legislative development in the ballroom case. The reconciliation vehicle (immigration enforcement bill) is designed to bypass Democratic filibuster — if Republicans hold together, it passes without Democratic support. Judge Leon's injunction blocking above-ground construction was premised on the absence of congressional approval; if this bill passes, it could moot the injunction, clearing the way for construction to resume. The 'non-security elements' bar is the legal fig leaf — but the underground military complex (which Judge Leon already permitted) was always the security core; the ballroom is the above-ground addition. Whether the $1B provision constitutes the 'congressional approval' Leon required is itself a legal question. Democrats are correct that this creates a midterm accountability moment: every senator goes on record on the ballroom. The WHCD shooting (050-A) is Trump's rhetorical justification; the timeline (June 1 deadline for the immigration bill) is aggressive. Connects to 038-B (triumphal arch, also seeking July groundbreaking) — both projects are being legislatively and administratively accelerated simultaneously in the lead-up to the 250th anniversary. GOVERNANCE NOTE: Democracy with significant authoritarian tendencies.

cases.title: Trump Triumphal Arch (proposed) — NYT sightline analysis; CFA post-approval revision letter
cases.institution: Columbia Island / Arlington Memorial Bridge approach, Washington DC
cases.description: UPDATE: The New York Times published a detailed 3-D model analysis on April 29 showing how the proposed 250-foot arch would affect sightlines between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington House (Robert E. Lee's mansion, built by enslaved people, atop Arlington National Cemetery). Key findings: from the Lincoln Memorial, the arch columns would frame Arlington House; from Arlington House, the arch would obscure much of the Lincoln Memorial. The reciprocal sightline between the two memorials was intentionally designed a century ago as a 'symbolic link between north and south' (NPS). Following its April 17 concept approval, the Commission of Fine Arts sent a letter backing the proposed location but endorsing only a smaller version — requesting removal of gilded statues at the top and more openings within columns to reduce obstruction of monumental views. NCPC approval still required; Trump has filled NCPC with allies. White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt has framed breaking ground as a 'fitting way' to commemorate America's 250th anniversary in July. Administration has not released cost details; expects combination of private and public funds, with construction to complete by end of Trump's term.
cases.outcome: CFA approved concept April 17 with revision requests (smaller, fewer gilded elements, more column openings). NCPC approval still required. Lawsuit pending. Administration targeting July groundbreaking.
cases.tags: Design controversy, Architectural preservation, Political art, Legal challenge, Funding dispute, Landmark dispute
cases.notes: The NYT 3-D model is the clearest visual demonstration of the sightline problem — the arch would obscure much of the Lincoln Memorial when viewed from Arlington House, inverting the intentional axial relationship the Memorial Bridge was designed to create. The CFA's post-approval revision requests (remove gilded statues; add column openings) are notable because they come from the body that already approved the concept — even Trump's own appointees are signaling the current design is too much. Priya Jain's framing — the reciprocal views are a 'guiding principle' and anything interrupting them 'should be very carefully considered' — is the scholarly standard the administration is bypassing. The NCPC is the remaining major approval hurdle; with Trump allies on that body, approval is likely but the process creates additional legal exposure if bypassed. Construction timeline (July 250th anniversary groundbreaking, completion by end of term) is the most ambitious in the DC monumental cluster. Cross-reference: 038/038-A (parent/CFA approval), 046 (Reflecting Pool), 050 (White House ballroom), 063 (National Garden of Heroes). GOVERNANCE NOTE: Democracy with significant authoritarian tendencies.

cases.title: Marine, Amsterdam (1874) / Adolphe Monet Reading in a Garden (1867) — Rouen hearing tomorrow
cases.institution: Tribunal judiciaire de Rouen
cases.description: STATUS CHECK: The Rouen court hearing in the Wildenstein/Monet 'vitiated consent' case is tomorrow, May 7, 2026. No pre-hearing developments identified. A March 2026 hearing at Rouen addressed a jurisdictional challenge from Wildenstein's attorney (Philippe Plantade), who contested the territorial competence of the Rouen tribunal and requested a postponement to March 26. The most recent Art Newspaper French edition reporting (March 23) confirms the jurisdiction challenge was addressed and a new hearing date was set for May 7. The sellers' claim: that Marine, Amsterdam's original canvas had been lost (replaced during transfer process) before the 2004 exchange, and that the gallery was likely aware of this — constituting a vice du consentement (vitiated consent) under French civil law that would nullify the entire exchange. If consent is vitiated: the 2004 transaction could be annulled, affecting Adolphe Monet Reading in a Garden (currently on loan at the Metropolitan Museum of Art) and Marine, Amsterdam (now owned by Larry Ellison). The sellers are represented by attorney Corinne Hershkovitch.
cases.outcome: Hearing May 7. Jurisdiction challenge previously addressed. No ruling yet. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING: search for outcome after May 7 hearing]
cases.tags: Authenticity, Legal challenge, Art market, Copyright/ownership
cases.notes: [FOLLOW-UP PENDING: hearing is tomorrow — search for outcome in next session] The jurisdiction challenge (Plantade contested Rouen's territorial competence) having been resolved in favor of the Rouen tribunal is itself a small procedural victory for the sellers. The Art Newspaper French edition's observation that the painting's signature changed between a 1892 photo and a 1957 photo — while the work was already in Wildenstein hands by 1974 — adds evidentiary texture to the 'gallery likely aware' finding. The nullification of the 2004 exchange would be one of the most consequential art market legal rulings in recent memory, affecting a work currently displayed at the Met. Search Friday.

cases.title: Loi-cadre sur la restitution des biens culturels spoliés — CMP underway; still unpromulgated
cases.institution: Assemblée nationale / Sénat / Élysée, Paris
cases.description: STATUS UPDATE: As of May 6, 2026, the repatriation framework law remains unpromulgated. The commission mixte paritaire (CMP) process to reconcile the Assemblée nationale's April 13 amended text with the Senate's January 2026 text is confirmed underway but no resolution or CMP date has been publicly announced. The key sticking point remains the RN-backed conditionality amendment requiring recipient states to commit to protecting and publicly displaying restituted objects — opposed by the government and the left. Minister Pégard noted approximately 10 current restitution requests, expected to grow significantly once the law is promulgated. The African Futures Lab joint statement (April 27) remains the most substantive external critique, noting the law avoids the word 'colonialism' and fails to acknowledge colonial violence.

cases.title: Slovak Arts Support Fund cancels €2M in active grants — Viva Musica! and 39 other projects
cases.artist: Multiple (Matej Drlička / Viva Musica!; BRaK literary festival; Dotyky a spojenia festival; 37 others)
cases.institution: Arts Support Fund (FPU); Slovak National Theatre and independent festivals, nationwide
cases.description: UPDATE: The Slovak Arts Support Fund canceled €2 million in multi-year grants for 40 active projects in March 2026 — mid-project, after work had already commenced. Projects affected include Viva Musica! festival (founded by Matej Drlička, who was dismissed from Slovak National Theatre directorship by Minister Šimkovičová); the BRaK literary festival; and the Dotyky a spojenia theatre festival in Martin. Drlička announced legal action. The March 2026 cancellations follow sweeping 2024 legislative changes that transferred final grant authority from expert committees to a 13-member council dominated by Culture Ministry nominees. Expert committees — previously central to decision-making — were reduced to advisory roles. Many experts refused to participate under the new rules, leaving the council without sufficient members to evaluate several 2026 programmes. Minister Šimkovičová defended the changes as improving transparency and eliminating a 'cash machine' for certain institutions. No-confidence motion against Šimkovičová failed February 2024; she remains in post as of May 6, 2026.
cases.outcome: Grants canceled. Drlička pursuing legal action. Arts Support Fund operating with diminished expert committee capacity. Minister remains in post.
cases.tags: Funding dispute, Censorship, Institutional crisis, Labor dispute, Political interference
cases.notes: [FOLLOW-UP PENDING] This is the financial mechanism completing the institutional capture pattern documented in entry 053. The sequence is now complete: (1) dismiss independent institution directors, (2) replace with political appointees, (3) restructure grant authority to ministry nominees, (4) cancel grants to independent projects mid-stream. The €2M cancellation mid-project is qualitatively different from defunding before a project begins — it strands artists and organizations who have already committed resources. Drlička's legal challenge is the first formal accountability action in the Slovak case. The Viva Musica! festival connection (founded by the dismissed SNT director) shows the minister continuing to target critics after their institutional removal. Compare: the Slovakia pattern is Hungary 2014 — exactly what Tisza now has the tools to reverse in Hungary. The Slovak Arts Council now lacks sufficient expert committee members to evaluate several 2026 funding programmes, creating institutional paralysis. GOVERNANCE NOTE: Democracy under sustained illiberal pressure (Fico coalition, 2023-present).

cases.title: 2026 Venice Biennale — ANGA strike announced May 8; preview opens
cases.institution: Venice Biennale, Giardini and Arsenale; Viale Garibaldi (rally site)
cases.description: ANGA announced a 24-hour cultural sector strike for May 8 (Friday), the first such organized strike within the Biennale. cases.title: Van Gogh Museum renovation funding dispute
cases.institution: Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam
cases.description: The Van Gogh Museum initiated legal proceedings against the Dutch government to demand an additional €2.5M annually toward a planned €104M renovation of its dated Amsterdam buildings, scheduled to begin in 2028. The museum's director, Emilie Gordenker, stated in August 2025 that without increased public subsidy the museum could be forced to close. The Dutch government (then under a different coalition) held that its existing €8.5M annual subsidy was sufficient and that costs beyond necessary maintenance were the museum's own responsibility. The Van Gogh Museum argues that under the 1962 agreement by which the Vincent van Gogh Foundation transferred more than 200 paintings, 500 drawings, and 900 letters to state stewardship, the Dutch government has a legal duty to construct and maintain a permanent museum. The case was due for a first hearing when both parties announced they had entered mediation and postponed legal proceedings. As of May 5, 2026 — under a new centre-left coalition (D66 PM Rob Jetten since February) — the Culture Minister Rianne Letschert confirmed the court granted an indefinite adjournment. Mediation is making 'good progress'; both parties aim to conclude before summer. Broader context: Dutch Council for Culture found public cultural funding fell from 0.47% to 0.35% of government spending between 2005 and 2023; smaller regional museums are struggling more acutely but lack the Van Gogh Museum's international press leverage. Museum had deliberately reduced visitors by a fifth to 1.8M annually; reported €2.9M profit and €2.3M donation increase in 2024.
cases.outcome: Legal proceedings postponed; mediation underway. Aim to conclude before summer 2026. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING]
cases.tags: Funding dispute, Legal challenge, Institutional crisis, Conservation
cases.notes: [FOLLOW-UP PENDING] Interesting structural case for Theme 2 and Theme 5. The 1962 agreement — family transfers the collection to state stewardship in exchange for a promise to build and maintain a permanent museum — is effectively a founding covenant now being litigated. The Van Gogh Museum's position (state must pay) vs. the government's (maintenance yes, improvements no) maps onto the broader question of what encyclopedic and national-patrimony museums are owed by states that claim them as cultural infrastructure. The political context matters: the previous coalition refused; a new centre-left coalition is now in mediation, suggesting political will may have shifted. The regional museum dimension is analytically important and underreported: smaller Dutch institutions without international brand recognition can't generate the press pressure the Van Gogh Museum can — the same structural funding decline is hitting them harder, silently. Dos Elshout's observation that the debate has become 'more negative because of right-wing sentiment' connects this to the broader European pattern of cultural funding under pressure (see entries 023/023-A for Germany, 026/026-A for Chile, 053 for Slovakia). Wednesday Europe/Francophone trawl. Enrich with Dutch-language sources.

cases.title: Marka27 / ICE-critical art exhibit — 'Institutional Critique' student off-campus response
cases.artist: Alexandra Elmendorf, Lynn May, Forest Nehemiah, Aidan Kearns, Lillie Hickman (UNT CVAD graduates)
cases.institution: 2 Bed 1 Bath (apartment gallery), Oak Cliff / Dallas TX; related: Dallas Latino Cultural Center
cases.description: Five UNT College of Visual Arts & Design graduates, citing low morale and fear of self-censorship following the Marka27 exhibit removal, organized an off-campus exhibition titled 'Institutional Critique' at a Dallas apartment converted into a gallery ('2 Bed 1 Bath') on April 25, 2026, with additional showings through May 3. Organizer Ryan Semegran said after the Marka27 removal, they felt 'embarrassed to have attended school there.' Student Alexandra Elmendorf: 'Our programs are supposed to be encouraging and help us explore critical thinking and emotional expression, whereas censorship makes us silence ourselves. Now people are scared and want to go with the status quo.' Student Lynn May: 'Morale here at CVAD has been incredibly low. No one's really happy and no one really wants to even put this school in their CV.' KERA News (May 1, 2026) coverage noted that Marka27's parallel show at the city-owned Dallas Latino Cultural Center ran through March 30 without incident — the municipal vs. university contrast remains stark. No reinstatement of the CVAD exhibition.
cases.outcome: Off-campus exhibition completed May 3. No reinstatement of CVAD Marka27 show. Chilling effect on students documented.
cases.tags: Censorship, Self-censorship, Institutional risk, Campus art, Campus censorship
cases.notes:
The student response enacts the critique the Marka27 removal was trying to suppress: they've named the show 'Institutional Critique,' opted out of campus spaces entirely, and documented exactly the chilling effects FIRE's William Harris warned about. The Dallas Latino Cultural Center contrast is the sharpest institutional example in the tracker: the same artist, shown without incident at a city-owned venue, censored at a state university. The students' reluctance to put UNT in their CVs is a concrete career consequence of institutional self-censorship. Direct pedagogical use: students taking a risk on their own professional futures to make the censorship visible. Cross-reference 011/011-A (Marka27 parent/ACLU billboard), 034 (NEA gutting), 049 (Pepperdine/Wende) for the chilling-effect cluster. GOVERNANCE NOTE: Democracy with significant authoritarian tendencies.

CAMPUS CENSORSHIP CLUSTER: Part of the tracker's documented pattern of university administrators removing or restricting art/speech through anticipatory obedience — citing procedural rationales (fire code, nonprofit status, campus disruption, funding risk) rather than content objections. Common mechanism: unilateral administrative action without consulting artists or faculty. cases.title: Iranian Pavilion — Venice Biennale 2026 withdrawal
cases.institution: Venice Biennale, Giardini
cases.description: The Islamic Republic of Iran withdrew from the 2026 Venice Biennale, announced today — hours before the professional preview opens. La Biennale's official statement confirmed: 'The Islamic Republic of Iran will not participate.' No reason was provided. Aydin Mahdizadeh Tehrani had been listed as commissioner for the planned Iranian pavilion. Iran returned to the Biennale in 2003 after a nearly three-decade absence and has participated in most editions since. Its 2024 pavilion, titled 'Of One Essence is the Human Race,' addressed women's rights under the Islamic Republic. The withdrawal brings the total number of notable absences to three: Iran (withdrawal), South Africa (official pavilion canceled by culture minister, artist showing independently at Chiesa di Sant'Antonin), and Russia (participating but pavilion closed to public for the entire run). The timing — announced the day of the preview opening — is notable.
cases.outcome: Iran has withdrawn. No official statement of reason. Preview opens today.
cases.tags: Geopolitics, Political interference, Censorship

Artnet
NATIVE: Khabar Online via ISNA (FA) — https://www.khabaronline.ir/news/2215062 ; Eco Iran via ISNA (FA) — https://ecoiran.com/بخش-فید-سیاسی-193/133535
cases.notes: No reason given — the silence is the story. The US-Israel-Iran conflict (entry 037) is the most plausible context: Iran's pavilion presence would have been politically uncomfortable given the active military conflict. The 2024 pavilion's women's rights theme adds a layer — 'Of One Essence is the Human Race' was the last Iranian cultural presentation before a war in which Iranian women's movement figures have continued to face repression. Three major absences now frame the 2026 Biennale's opening: Iran (withdrawn), South Africa (empty official pavilion), Russia (present but sealed). Cross-reference 008-L (pre-opening status), 008-M (today's Venice update), 037 (Iran war cultural heritage destruction). GOVERNANCE NOTE: Iran is a theocratic authoritarian state. The withdrawal of the Iranian pavilion may represent state censorship of outward cultural display during wartime — a different dynamic from the democratic-nation controversies elsewhere in this cluster.

cases.title: Trump Kennedy Center Renaming / Artist Boycott
cases.institution: Kennedy Center, Washington DC; US District Court (Judge Christopher Cooper)
cases.description: UPDATE: Judge Christopher Cooper (USDC for DC) held back-to-back hearings April 28–29 on the two separate Kennedy Center lawsuits — the Beatty lawsuit (renaming and closure) and the preservation groups' lawsuit (architectural preservation and federal review requirements). Cooper grilled both sides extensively. Key exchange in the Beatty hearing: Cooper asked the government's attorney Brantley Mayers where in any submission was the administration's analysis of the costs of total two-year closure versus alternatives such as phased or partial closure. 'I didn't see any numbers,' Cooper said. Cooper also asked why the government opposes phasing renovations around performances, which had been the 'status quo' until the recent abrupt reversal. For the preservation groups, Cooper questioned what legal framework requires the administration to observe federal historic preservation requirements for changes to the KC, including painting columns white, cutting down weeping willows, and adding Trump's name without Section 106, NCPC, or CFA review. Cooper took no action at either hearing. Ruling pending. Separately: Kennedy Center officials at the April 22 media tour acknowledged the building will look 'largely the same' after two years; confirmed Reach extension will remain partially open; said only skeleton staff retained during closure.
cases.outcome: Hearings completed April 28–30. No ruling yet. Closure still July 4. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING: Cooper ruling expected — could issue injunction blocking closure or name change.]
cases.tags: Political interference, Institutional crisis, Legal challenge, Architectural preservation
cases.notes: [FOLLOW-UP PENDING] Cooper's question 'I didn't see any numbers' is the strongest signal yet that he may issue a ruling requiring the administration to justify the total-closure decision procedurally. The preservation groups added new detail at the April 30 hearing: changes already made (column repainting, willow tree removal, name addition) were made without any Section 106 consultation, NCPC review, or CFA input — all required for modifications to nationally significant historic properties. The administration's counter-argument: these were maintenance decisions within board authority. If Cooper issues an injunction before July 4 closing date, it would be the most consequential legal check on the Kennedy Center situation yet. GOVERNANCE NOTE: Democracy with significant authoritarian tendencies.
cases.interested_parties: Judge Christopher Cooper (USDC); Rep. Joyce Beatty (Beatty lawsuit); Norm Eisen / Nathaniel Zelinsky (Beatty counsel); National Trust for Historic Preservation / DC Preservation League / AIA (preservation lawsuit); Greg Werkheiser (preservation counsel); Brantley Mayers (DOJ attorney); Matt Floca (KC executive director)

cases.title: Iryna Zarutska Memorial Murals (nationwide)

cases.title: Primera Bienal de Arte Indígena de Buenos Aires — Gran Chaco exhibition cancellation
cases.artist: 46 Indigenous artists (Wichí, Qom, Moqoit and others from Argentina, Peru, Paraguay, Brazil, Chile)
cases.institution: Palacio Libertad (formerly Centro Cultural Kirchner), Buenos Aires; Pabellón de Bellas Artes UCA, Puerto Madero
cases.description: Argentina's Secretaría de Cultura de la Nación (headed by Leonardo Cifelli under Milei) canceled the satellite Wichí/Gran Chaco component of the First Bienal de Arte Indígena de Buenos Aires two days before its scheduled installation in Sala 606 of the Palacio Libertad, citing 'programming changes.' The Bienal itself — organized by the Fundación Redes Solidarias and running at the UCA Pabellón de Bellas Artes February 11 – April 12, 2026 — featured 46 Indigenous artists from northern Argentina and four neighboring countries. The Palacio Libertad is the renamed former Centro Cultural Kirchner. The Secretaría also required the Bienal's main text panels not to use the word 'indígena' and prohibited display of the organizing network's logos. The Chaco show was relocated to Espacio Vitriol (Perón 1253); some large-format works could not be displayed there. Organizer Mercedes Avellaneda de Bocca: 'Fue un acto de discriminación y censura.' The Bienal's main exhibition — which distributed prizes totaling 4.1M pesos — proceeded at UCA without government interference. A co-located exhibition at the Palacio Libertad's ground-floor artisan market (Sueños y visiones) was permitted to continue.
cases.outcome: Chaco exhibition cancellation stands. Main Bienal completed its run through April 12 at UCA without further interference. No legal challenge.
