cases.title: "Nude Laughing" (2014–); "Subvert, Repair, Reclaim: Contemporary Artists Take Back the Nude" (exhibition)
cases.institution: Museum of Fine Arts Boston, Boston, Massachusetts
cases.description: Artist Xandra Ibarra performed 'Nude Laughing' (2014–) at the MFA Boston on April 16 as part of 'Subvert, Repair, Reclaim: Contemporary Artists Take Back the Nude,' a 12-artist exhibition critiquing racial, gender, and power hierarchies in the Western art canon. Ibarra appeared nude except for an artificial breastplate and yellow heels, walking through the galleries — including the Art of Europe section — trailing a stocking stuffed with 'white lady accoutrements' (blonde wigs, hyperfeminine accessories, fake breasts), culminating in hysterics in front of Gauguin's 'Where Do We Come From? What Are We? Where Are We Going?' The performance ran ~20 minutes; audience lingered 30 minutes after. Museum posted photo documentation to Instagram, igniting a comment-section controversy: hundreds called it 'disgusting,' 'vulgar,' 'exhibitionist,' 'public indecency,' and 'a mockery to the history of art.' One commenter threatened to cancel her museum membership. However, the MFA confirmed only two people formally contacted the museum to complain. The museum held firm — no cancellation, no apology.
cases.outcome: Performance completed. Museum held firm. No formal cancellation or retraction. Online controversy ongoing.
cases.tags: Community objection, Obscenity, Public objection, Performance art
cases.notes: The most analytically interesting feature is what didn't happen: in the current climate of institutional self-censorship (entries 011, 018, 027, 031, 044, 051), the MFA Boston ran the performance with adequate warnings and declined to apologize despite social media pressure. Only 2 formal complaints vs. hundreds of online comments — a useful data point about the gap between social media outrage and actual public mobilization. The performance's staging in front of the Gauguin is precisely chosen: Gauguin's Pacific nude paintings are among the most canonical examples of the male-gaze colonial nude, and Ibarra laughing hysterically at them while herself nude inverts the power relationship those paintings encode. Curator Hermo's framing — the proposal was 'really centered around why it should be at the MFA Boston, this encyclopedic museum that has so much colonial baggage' — is Theme 5 (Ethical Museum) language. Direct counterweight to the self-censorship cluster; teach alongside 044 (SMoCA transfeminisms) as opposite institutional responses to pressure. The two-complaints-vs-hundreds-online ratio is itself ARTH 201 material on Theme 9: when the public objects, which public?
cases.interested_parties: Xandra Ibarra (artist), Carmen Hermo (MFA Boston curator, Contemporary Art), MFA Boston, Instagram commenters, museum members and general public

cases.title: "30 Mil Motivos" (mural)
cases.institution: Centro Cultural Osvaldo Soriano / Biblioteca Municipal Leopoldo Marechal, Mar del Plata, Buenos Aires Province
cases.description: UPDATE: Opposition bloc Unión por la Patria formally filed a project in the Concejo Deliberante requesting: (1) that the municipal executive explain who authorized the paint-over and whether permits were obtained; (2) whether cultural heritage protection norms were violated; (3) an official apology to Freites's family and human rights organizations; (4) commitment to restoration. The 0223 local outlet confirmed the project reached the Concejo. The municipal government's defense is that the wall belongs to a private residence and the intervention was maintenance for water filtration damage. Madres de Plaza de Mayo and Abuelas de Plaza de Mayo were formally invited by concejal Centurión to participate in coordinating restoration. Multiple national Argentine outlets covered the case.
cases.outcome: Concejo Deliberante project filed. Municipal government denies responsibility. Restoration not yet commenced. Investigation pending.
cases.tags: Vandalism, Historical erasure, Community objection, Removal, Political interference
cases.notes: The opposition's formal project in the Concejo confirms this escalated beyond social media outrage to institutional action. The private-wall defense vs. civic heritage claim is the central legal question. The Madres/Abuelas invitation is significant: in Argentina, their institutional involvement transforms a local mural dispute into a national memory-politics event. Note the date: the intervention was discovered near the anniversary of the March 24, 1976 coup (Día Nacional de la Memoria), adding another layer to the charge that this was politically timed. Connects to entry 013 (Milei/Buenos Aires exhibition censorship) and broader Milei governance pattern.

cases.title: N/A (systemic / multiple educational resources and programming)
cases.institution: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum (USHMM), Washington DC
cases.description: The USHMM quietly removed educational resources connecting Nazi racial ideology to American racism (Jim Crow) from its website, unlisted a 2018 YouTube video of a Holocaust survivor in conversation with a woman whose father was lynched in Alabama, and renamed then canceled a college workshop on 'Fragility of Democracy and the Rise of the Nazis' — changed to 'Before the Holocaust: German Society and the Nazi Rise to Power.' Two former employees told Politico they believed the changes were preemptive, intended to avoid the kind of attack Trump launched against the Smithsonian. Trump had not publicly commented on the USHMM. In March 2026, Trump replaced long-serving founding board chair Stuart Eizenstat with Republican lobbyist Jeffrey Miller. Museum denied any retreat from content or Trump administration direction. Sen. Jacky Rosen (D-NV), a Holocaust Memorial Council member, said she would raise questions within the council.
cases.outcome: Content removed. Workshop canceled. Leadership replaced. Museum denies self-censorship.
cases.tags: Censorship, Self-censorship, Historical erasure, Political interference, Institutional risk
cases.notes: The USHMM case is the most symbolically significant entry in the self-censorship cluster. An institution dedicated to the warning 'Never Again' quietly erasing materials about the connections between Nazi racial policy and American Jim Crow law is the clearest possible illustration of the 'anticipatory obedience' pattern documented in entries 018 (Art Museum of the Americas), 027 (Sherald/Smithsonian), and 044 (SMoCA). The renaming of 'Fragility of Democracy' is itself a teaching text: the internal email explains the word 'fragility' raised 'concerns regarding how the term may be perceived in the current climate.' A Holocaust museum is now self-censoring language about democratic fragility in 2026. The Eizenstat replacement with a Republican lobbyist — removing one of the institution's founders — follows the Kennedy Center governance capture pattern. Connect to entries 005 (Kennedy Center), 012 (Smithsonian), 034 (NEA). GOVERNANCE NOTE: Democracy with significant authoritarian tendencies.

cases.title: White House Correspondents Dinner shooting / ballroom rationale
cases.institution: Washington Hilton, Washington DC
cases.description: On the evening of April 25, 2026, gunman Cole Tomas Allen (31, Torrance, California) stormed the White House Correspondents Dinner at the Washington Hilton, armed with a shotgun, handgun, and multiple knives. Allen ran past the main magnetometer security checkpoint near the ballroom stairs and exchanged fire with Secret Service agents; one agent was struck in a bullet-resistant vest and is expected to recover. No other injuries. Allen taken into custody. Acting AG Todd Blanche told CNN the suspect appeared to be targeting Trump administration officials. Trump, Melania, VP Vance, and cabinet members were evacuated to a secure area; Trump departed at approximately 9:45 PM. Approximately 2,600 attendees including RFK Jr., Rubio, Kash Patel, and Lee Zeldin were present. This was the first WHCA Dinner Trump attended as a sitting president. Security note: Washington Hilton lobby remained open to regular hotel guests during the dinner, per standard practice; security screening was located inside at the checkpoint directly outside the ballroom rather than at hotel entrance. At a press conference afterward, Trump almost immediately cited the venue's security as rationale for the White House Ballroom, calling the Washington Hilton "not a particularly secure building" and using the incident as justification for having a dedicated presidential events venue. Trump also said the shooting would not stop him from "winning the war in Iran."
cases.outcome: Suspect in custody; arraignment Monday April 27. Motive under investigation. Ballroom construction injunction still in effect.
cases.tags: Security failure, Political interference, Design controversy, Landmark dispute
cases.notes: The operative analytical fact here is the speed and directness of Trump's pivot: a security incident at a commercial hotel became, within hours, public justification for a $400M+ publicly funded vanity construction project currently under federal court injunction. This is the clearest statement yet of the ballroom's actual political logic: not state dinners, but a controlled, dedicated presidential venue that removes the executive from public and commercial spaces. The Washington Hilton's security arrangement -- open lobby, checkpoint at the ballroom perimeter -- is standard for the venue and was described by former FBI deputy director Andrew McCabe as "almost on the level of a national security event" given the concentration of officials. Whether Trump's characterization of it as insufficiently secure is accurate or is opportunistic framing is the question. The ballroom has been enjoined by federal courts precisely because Congress has not authorized it; Trump is now using a security incident to build public pressure for a project a judge found has no legal basis. This is worth tracking as a rhetorical strategy: court injunction -> security incident -> renewed public justification -> political pressure on Congress. Not a traditional art controversy, but directly relevant to the architectural preservation and public funding cluster. GOVERNANCE NOTE: Democracy with significant authoritarian tendencies.
cases.interested_parties: Cole Tomas Allen (suspect, 31, Torrance CA), Trump, Melania, VP Vance, cabinet (evacuated), Acting AG Todd Blanche, Secret Service Director Sean Curran, DC interim Police Chief Jeffery Carroll, CNN's Wolf Blitzer (eyewitness), White House Correspondents Association

cases.title: White House State Ballroom / East Wing demolition
cases.artist: McCrery Architects (Jim McCrery, lead); Clark Construction; AECOM (engineering)
cases.institution: White House East Wing site, Washington DC
cases.description: In July 2025, Trump announced plans to demolish the White House East Wing and replace it with an 89,000 sq ft state ballroom, framed as providing a larger venue than the East Room for state dinners. McCrery Architects (classical design firm) selected as lead; Clark Construction as builder; AECOM as engineer. Cost announced at $200M, rose to $300-400M by October 2025. Trump said private donors and corporations would pay; construction began September 2025 and continued through the October 2025 federal government shutdown (OMB memo confirmed private funding). East Wing demolished October 20, 2025 -- demolition became an impromptu tourist attraction; Presidential Emergency Operations Center (WWII-era underground bunker) dismantled as part of site prep. Design problems widely reported: exterior grand staircase leading to a wall with no door, columns blocking sightlines, fake windows, staircase breaking symmetry of Olmsted-designed 1930s driveway. NYT published design flaw critique March 29, 2026; Trump revealed revised design the next day. National Trust for Historic Preservation sued December 2025 for failure to observe federal historic preservation guidelines. DOJ argued February 2026 that halting construction raised "national security implications." NCPC approved final design 8-1 on April 2, 2026. Judge Richard Leon issued preliminary injunction March 31 halting above-ground construction, finding no law "comes close" to giving Trump authority to build such a structure without Congressional approval. Revised April 16 order: above-ground construction blocked; below-ground work (including classified military complex) permitted. Trump confirmed a "massive complex" being built underground; Secret Service said pausing would "hamper its statutory obligations." FY2026 White House renovation budget: $377M (866% increase from FY2025). ADAO filed FOIA lawsuit over asbestos inspection records. Rose Garden previously paved with stone patio (2025). White House Correspondents Dinner shooting April 25, 2026: Trump immediately cited venue security as rationale for ballroom -- see entry 050-A.
cases.outcome: Above-ground construction enjoined (April 16 order). Below-ground/national security work proceeding. NTHP lawsuit active. ADAO FOIA lawsuit active. NCPC approved final design April 2. Appeals ongoing.
cases.tags: Design controversy, Architectural preservation, Demolition, Landmark dispute, Funding dispute, Legal challenge, Political art, Historical erasure
cases.notes: [FOLLOW-UP PENDING] This is a significant legal and political setback for the ballroom project. The legislative strategy behind 050-B was to use the reconciliation bill to (a) fund the project without Democratic votes, and (b) provide the 'congressional approval' Judge Leon identified as lacking when he issued his injunction. The parliamentarian's ruling knocks out both objectives simultaneously: the money is gone (for now), and the congressional authorization rationale collapses with it. Republicans can restructure, but any restructured provision faces either the same parliamentary challenge or a 60-vote threshold Democrats will not provide. The Secret Service's own breakdown — $220M directly to White House project, $780M to other security programs — inadvertently confirmed that most of the $1B was not actually ballroom-related, which may have undermined the 'security' rationale that was the provision's legal fig leaf. Democrats' plan to force repeated ballroom votes is a midterm strategy: every Republican senator on record supporting Trump's vanity project. Judge Leon's injunction remains in effect; without the legislative clear Judge Leon required, above-ground construction stays blocked. Cross-reference 050 (parent entry), 050-A (WHCD shooting as ballroom rationale), 050-B (provision inserted), 038-C (triumphal arch no-bid contract parallel). GOVERNANCE NOTE: Democracy with significant authoritarian tendencies.

cases.title: 2026 Venice Biennale: Golden Lion jury ICC exclusion statement
cases.artist: Jury: Solange Farkas (chair), Elvira Dyangani Ose, Zoe Butt, Marta Kuzma, Giovanna Zapperi
cases.institution: Venice Biennale, Giardini and Arsenale
cases.description: The five-member jury for the 2026 Venice Biennale announced April 23-24 that it will not consider for the Golden Lion or Silver Lion awards any national pavilion whose country's leaders are currently charged with crimes against humanity by the International Criminal Court. The statement does not name countries but directly affects Russia (Putin under ICC arrest warrant for Ukraine war crimes) and Israel (Netanyahu under ICC arrest warrant for Gaza). The jury framed the decision as consistent with the late Koyo Kouoh's curatorial vision for In Minor Keys. The Biennale's press office distanced itself, noting the jury acts autonomously. Israeli artist Belu-Simion Fainaru responded that the jury's action created a hostile and degrading environment and constitutes discrimination based on national origin, noting that the Biennale's own stated policy rejects exclusion. ANGA praised the decision but criticized the jury for not naming Israel explicitly and invited jurors to sign ANGA's open letter (now 200 signatories). Finland's political boycott of the Russian pavilion remains in place. Hyperallergic's guide to the Biennale also confirmed the US was named in the ANGA open letter (along with Israel and Russia) -- unprecedented triple exclusion demand.
cases.outcome: Jury exclusion from awards announced April 23. Both pavilions proceeding. Preview opens May 6.
cases.tags: Geopolitics, Protest, Boycott, Institutional risk
cases.notes: The jury's move creates a split within the Biennale's own structure: the institution says it cannot exclude any country recognized by Italy; the jury says it can refuse to award them. This is internal institutional dissent that stops short of exclusion but imposes a meaningful symbolic penalty. Fainaru's objection is legally interesting -- he is correct that the Biennale's anti-exclusion policy is contradicted by the jury's action, even if the jury acts autonomously. The ICC criterion is also theoretically unstable: Afghanistan's leaders are also under ICC warrants but Afghanistan has no pavilion; other states with serious violations are not affected. Compare Theme 6 (When is iconoclasm/exclusion justified? Can a consistent standard be applied?): the jury has articulated a standard (ICC charges) that would not apply equally in all analogous cases. Nine days to preview opening (May 6). This is the most consequential Venice development this week. GOVERNANCE NOTE: Israel is formally a democracy but characterized by UN Special Rapporteurs, Amnesty International, and Human Rights Watch as operating an apartheid regime in the occupied Palestinian territories.

cases.title: Hold My Hand in Yours exhibition
cases.artist: Elana Mann; AMBOS (Art Made Between Opposite Sides); 12+ artists
cases.institution: Frederick R. Weisman Museum of Art, Pepperdine University, Malibu, California
cases.description: Pepperdine University administrators visited the Weisman Museum on October 1, 2025, and directed that two works be turned off or obscured as overtly political content: Elana Mann's video Call to Arms 2015-2025 (a decade-spanning documentation of protest performances using arm-shaped megaphones) and AMBOS's Con Nuestros Manos Construimos Deidades, a collaborative sculpture by 240+ people including refugees and asylum-seekers near the US-Mexico border, which included an embroidered patch reading "Save the Children" and "Abolish ICE." University cited longstanding practice of avoiding political content consistent with its nonprofit status. Both artists withdrew their work. At least 12 other artists withdrew in solidarity, forcing early closure of the exhibition (originally scheduled through March 2026). Museum director Andrea Gyorody resigned October 24. Pepperdine Fine Arts faculty issued statement of full support for the artists. NCAC and College Art Association issued joint open letter calling the nonprofit-status rationale "misguided and untenable." Case resurfaced April 26, 2026 when Wende Museum (Culver City, CA) premiered Mann's related performance Whirlwinds, Tornadoes, Basement at its Spring 2026 opening, explicitly noting it as a work recently removed by administrators at Pepperdine's Weisman Museum after being deemed political in nature.
cases.outcome: Exhibition closed early October 2025. Director resigned. NCAC/CAA letters sent. No restoration. Mann's related work premiering at Wende Museum today, April 26.
cases.tags: Censorship, Self-censorship, Institutional risk, Campus art, Political interference, Campus censorship
cases.notes:
Surfaced today via Wende Museum Spring 2026 opening, which explicitly frames the Mann performance as the work censored at Pepperdine. The Pepperdine administration's rationale -- that displaying political art threatens the university's nonprofit status -- was called "disingenuous" by NCAC because displaying an artwork is not the same as institutional endorsement. Pattern companion to 011 (UNT/Marka27), 031 (UNC mural), 044 (SMoCA transfeminisms): university/nonprofit self-censors to protect institutional standing. The Wende Museum, which specializes in Cold War-era cultural history, presenting the work today is its own meta-commentary: the institution that documents authoritarian censorship of art is where the censored art now premieres. Students: compare Pepperdine's "nonprofit status" defense to UNT's "campus disruption" defense -- both are institutional survival framings that bypass the content question entirely. GOVERNANCE NOTE: Democracy with significant authoritarian tendencies. Executive action on cultural institutions exceeds normal democratic norms.

CAMPUS CENSORSHIP CLUSTER: Part of the tracker's documented pattern of university administrators removing or restricting art/speech through anticipatory obedience — citing procedural rationales (fire code, nonprofit status, campus disruption, funding risk) rather than content objections. Common mechanism: unilateral administrative action without consulting artists or faculty. See entries 011/011-A/011-B (UNT/Marka27), 031 (UNC Chapel Hill), 049 (Pepperdine/Wende), 087 (UC Berkeley MCC). Dallas Latino Cultural Center contrast (011) is the cleanest institutional variable: same artist, same work, no interference at a city-owned venue. cases.description: A pattern of cultural self-censorship has deepened in India under Prime Minister Narendra Modi's BJP government, documented in multiple 2026 reports. cases.title: National Museum of Sudan and 20+ additional museums and cultural sites
cases.institution: National Museum of Sudan, Ethnographic Museum, Natural History Museum, Khalifa House Museum, Nyala Museum, El Geneina Museum (Khartoum and Darfur region)
cases.description: The Sudanese civil war (2023–present) has caused destruction and looting of more than 20 museums, with financial damage exceeding $110 million. The Rapid Support Forces (RSF) occupied the National Museum of Sudan in June 2023, looting over 100,000 archaeological artefacts including ancient gold, jewellery, and ceremonial items from the Napatan and Meroitic civilizations. By March 2026, approximately 60–90% of the National Museum's holdings had been destroyed or removed (varying estimates from NCAM director Ghalia Garelnabi). Looted objects have appeared for sale on eBay and through European and African art dealers. In February 2026, the RSF was accused of burning the library of the College of Forestry at Sudan University of Science and Technology and using musical instruments as fuel. SAF forces recaptured Khartoum in March 2025; January 13, 2026, some recovered artefacts were displayed in a ceremony in Port Sudan. UNESCO has documented 1,700+ objects, trained police and customs officers, and appealed to international institutions. ICRC condemned attacks. Lack of media coverage compared to Afghanistan and Iraq has limited international responsiveness.
cases.outcome: Ongoing. Some artefacts recovered and displayed January 2026. SAF retook Khartoum March 2025. Museum interior destroyed. UNESCO documentation ongoing. No accountability proceedings. UNESCO implementation underway (see 047-B): five priority museums assessed (Kerma, Gebel Barkal, Red Sea, El Damer, Sennar), 1,737 artefacts digitally inventoried, El Damer collection relocated to Kerma, 500 heritage/customs/judiciary professionals trained (reported May 18, 2026).

cases.title: Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool renovation
cases.institution: National Mall, Washington DC
cases.description: President Trump announced on April 23 that renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool is already underway. He described the pool as filthy and dirty and said a friend prompted his inspection. Trump toured the site with Secret Service and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum. A contractor proposed removing and replacing the granite at a cost of $300M over three years; Trump rejected this and instead called contractors from his real estate career, who agreed to resurface the pool for $1.5M-$2M. Work began two weeks prior to the announcement. Trump chose the color American flag blue for the new industrial-grade pool coating. The pool was last renovated in 2012 at a cost of approximately $30M. The reflecting pool is a National Historic Landmark and site of major civil rights and antiwar protests including Martin Luther King Jr.'s I Have a Dream speech (1963) and the 1971 Vietnam War protests. No Section 106 review, congressional approval, or National Capital Planning Commission process has been publicly announced. The renovation follows Trump's demolition of the White House East Wing (halted by federal court), the proposed triumphal arch (CFA approved April 17), and the White House Rose Garden paving.
cases.outcome: Renovation underway. No legal challenge filed yet. No public review process announced.

cases.title: Loi-cadre sur la restitution des biens culturels spoliés durant la colonisation
cases.institution: Assemblée nationale and Senate, Paris; French museums; Mali, Algeria, Benin, Ivory Coast
cases.description: UPDATE: Additional coverage confirms the April 13 unanimous National Assembly vote (170 votes). cases.title: transfeminisms / "There are other skies"
cases.artist: Zainab Fasiki, Alex Martinis Roe, Fatima Mazmouz, Ada Pinkston, Bahia Shehab, Lorena Wolffer, Cassils, Martine Gutierrez, and others
cases.institution: Scottsdale Museum of Contemporary Art (SMoCA), Scottsdale, Arizona
cases.description: A traveling feminist exhibition originated by Mimosa House (London) as 'transfeminisms' — a major survey of women, queer, and trans artists — was significantly altered before opening at SMoCA. The exhibition was retitled 'There are other skies,' shortened by two months, and had its artist lineup reduced. Chief curator Jennifer McCabe resigned from SMoCA in October 2024, and co-curators (Daria Khan, Maura Reilly) say they were sidelined after her departure and told of changes without input. Khan: the show was 'violently edited.' SMoCA CEO Gerd Wuestemann maintains changes were 'pragmatic' and driven by space, budget, and timeline constraints. Context: Scottsdale City Council had voted to cut DEI funding; Arizona legislature introduced anti-trans bills in the same session. The case entered national discourse when NBC News cited it as part of a pattern of LGBTQ art censorship at US museums in August 2025.
cases.outcome: Exhibition shown in altered form. No retraction or restoration. Case now part of documented national pattern.
cases.tags: Censorship, Self-censorship, Institutional risk, Funding dispute
cases.notes: Surfaced in Wednesday dragnet as part of NBC News LGBTQ art censorship pattern story. This is a 2025 case that should have been logged earlier — backdating Date Discovered to reflect when it first appeared in tracker-relevant coverage (NBC News August 2025). The 'pragmatic vs. censorship' framing is important for class: SMoCA's institutional defense is identical to the V&A's 'minor edits' defense. The distinction between curatorial adaptation (legitimate) and ideologically driven alteration (censorship) is exactly what ARTH 201 Theme 4 explores. Compare to entry 011 (UNT/Marka27), 027 (Sherald/Smithsonian), and 031 (UNC mural) for a US institutional self-censorship cluster.

cases.title: Basma al-Sharif censorship chain (Goethe-Institut / Düsseldorf / Osnabrück)
cases.institution: EMAF (European Media Art Festival), Kunsthalle Osnabrück
cases.description: UPDATE: The 39th EMAF (European Media Art Festival) opened today, April 22, in Osnabrück. Al-Sharif's short film 'Morning Circle' (Morgenkreis) is being screened despite ongoing political controversy. Landschaftsverband Osnabrücker Land joined the city of Osnabrück and Lower Saxony PM Lies in publicly distancing from the festival over al-Sharif's inclusion. Festival director Katrin Mundt defended the decision on grounds of artistic freedom: 'We have shown her films for years. They were selected not only by us but also by Jewish Israelis.' City of Osnabrück confirmed its €150,000 annual funding remains intact. The WSWS (April 16) published analysis characterizing the Foreign Ministry's reprimand of the Goethe-Institut as 'coded language for censorship and repression.' The festival theme is 'An Incomplete Assembly' — the irony that an exhibition about incomplete assemblies is itself under pressure for assembling Palestinian voices was noted in the taz.
cases.outcome: Festival open April 22–26. Al-Sharif film showing. Patronage withdrawn. Funding intact. Multiple governmental bodies distancing from festival.
cases.tags: Censorship, Political interference, Funding dispute, Self-censorship
cases.notes: This is live today: the festival opened this morning in Osnabrück. The pattern is now three-stage: Goethe-Institut reprimanded (retroactive punishment), Düsseldorf Academy pressured (institutional capitulation with partial resistance), Osnabrück distancing (governmental disapproval without defunding). Each step documents the architecture of soft censorship: no one bans the work, but the cost of showing it is made progressively higher. The Mundt defense — 'we've shown her films for years, selected by Jewish Israelis too' — is the most direct pushback yet in this case. The EMAF theme 'An Incomplete Assembly' addressing how institutions manage power and language is an extraordinary coincidence; the festival is living its own theme.
cases.interested_parties: Basma al-Sharif, Katrin Mundt (EMAF director), City of Osnabrück, Landschaftsverband Osnabrücker Land, Lower Saxony PM Olaf Lies (withdrew patronage), German Foreign Ministry, taz, WSWS

cases.title: Post-Orbán de-politicization of Hungarian cultural institutions
cases.institution: Hungarian state broadcaster MTVA; Hungarian Academy of Arts; Budapest cultural institutions broadly
cases.description: UPDATE: Prime minister-elect Magyar announced within days of election victory that he will suspend state media news broadcasts until independent standards are restored. In a combative April 16 appearance on state TV M1, Magyar compared the broadcaster's coverage to 'North Korean' and 'Goebbels'-style propaganda and called it a 'factory of lies.' Plans to pass new media law creating independent media authority. 90 MTI state news agency journalists publicly demanded editorial independence. Cabinet expected to be sworn in by mid-May 2026. On cultural institutions specifically: no major appointments announced yet as of April 22; Tisza's supermajority gives it constitutional power to restructure the Hungarian Academy of Arts (MMA), which Orbán had elevated constitutionally. EU unlocking €17B in frozen funds tied to rule-of-law conditionality discussed in Brussels April 18.
cases.outcome: Government transition. State broadcaster suspension announced. Cabinet formation mid-May. Cultural institution restructuring pending.
cases.tags: Political interference, Institutional crisis, Censorship, Funding dispute, Self-censorship
cases.notes:
The state broadcaster suspension is itself a governance action worth tracking — Magyar's approach mirrors Poland's Tusk (TVP Info taken off air 2023), which remains contested. The parallel with the Polish outcome is cautionary: Polish public media put into liquidation but still operating after presidential veto of funding. The cultural institutions question (MMA, Ludwig Museum) remains the pending story: no director changes yet but supermajority gives Magyar the tools. The US parallel is explicit — CNN and NBC both note Trump's cultural policies followed the Orbán blueprint; now Hungary shows whether the blueprint can be reversed.

cases.title: Arthur Ashe Memorial Mural
cases.artist: Hamilton Glass (and Sir James Thornhill, restorer)
cases.institution: Battery Park, Richmond, Virginia (Arthur Ashe tunnel, Dupont Circle)
cases.description: A federal judge ordered Patriot Front, its founder Thomas Rousseau, and members William Ring and Jacob Brown to pay over $470,000 in punitive damages for the October 2021 defacement of a mural honoring Richmond-born tennis legend and civil rights activist Arthur Ashe in the majority-Black Battery Park neighborhood. Patriot Front members spray-painted the mural with white nationalist logos and stickers, caught on video they filmed themselves. The lawsuit, filed in 2022 by the Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under Law on behalf of Battery Park residents, argued the vandalism was intended to intimidate Black residents and violated their civil rights under the Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871. Patriot Front advocates for a white ethnostate. Battery Park residents testified to anxiety and stress when accessing the park after the attack. The mural had been restored in 2022 by Sir James Thornhill, one of the original artists. Civil penalties against the group aim to disrupt Patriot Front's organizing network.
cases.outcome: Judgment entered April 2026. $470,000+ punitive damages ordered. Mural restored (2022). Criminal charges not filed — McEachin's office declined.
cases.tags: Vandalism, Racial/ethnic sensitivity, Legal challenge, White nationalism
outlets: Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under Law
cases.notes: Richmond standing search. Battery Park is the neighborhood where Ashe learned to play tennis as a child — the mural is in the park itself, making the attack an erasure of local identity at its source. The $470K figure is significant as civil accountability for mural vandalism is uncommon; compare to 5Pointz ($6.75M, entry 010) as a different VARA route. The Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871 as the legal vehicle is interesting — a Reconstruction-era civil rights statute being used in 2026 to protect public art in a majority-Black Richmond neighborhood. McEachin declining criminal charges while a civil court awarded substantial damages creates an interesting split accountability. Direct proximity to VCU (15 min) — students can visit Battery Park.

cases.title: "30 Mil Motivos" (mural)
cases.institution: Centro Cultural Osvaldo Soriano / Biblioteca Municipal Leopoldo Marechal, 25 de Mayo al 3100, Mar del Plata, Buenos Aires Province
cases.description: A mural by the late Mar del Plata artist Osmar Freites, created in 2014 to commemorate the 30,000 people disappeared during Argentina's last military dictatorship (1976–1983), was painted over in its entirety with white paint. Freites, deeply committed to human rights work, died in 2015. The mural was located on the exterior wall adjacent to the city's public cultural center and library. Councilmember Melisa Centurión (Acción Marplatense) accused the local municipal government — aligned with the Milei national government — of 'insólito vandalism' against collective memory. The municipal government denied direct responsibility, claiming the wall belongs to a private residence and that paint-over occurred during routine maintenance. Opposition bloc (Unión por la Patria) introduced a project in the Concejo Deliberante demanding investigation of possible cultural heritage crimes, an official apology to Freites's family and human rights organizations, and restoration of the work. Centurión invoked the language of 'blanqueamiento' (whitewashing) — both literal and figurative.
cases.outcome: Mural painted over. Investigation project filed in Concejo Deliberante. Municipal government denies responsibility.
cases.tags: Vandalism, Historical erasure, Community objection, Removal, Political interference
cases.notes:
Connects directly to entry 013 (Milei government and Buenos Aires cultural censorship). The 'blanqueamiento' framing — painting over a memorial to the disappeared — carries extra weight in Argentine political culture where literal and figurative erasure of memory is a live political issue. The dispute over whether the wall is 'private' (municipality's defense) or publicly significant (opposition's position) is a classic threshold question for cultural heritage protection with no applicable law yet. Centurión's explicit linkage to 'ideological alignment with Milei' positions this within a broader pattern of memory-erasure under Argentina's far-right turn. The artist is deceased, so no VARA-equivalent claim exists — this is purely a civic and political battle. Monday Latin America trawl. Enrich next Monday.

cases.title: New Deal murals and site-specific artworks in four DC federal buildings (Ben Shahn, Philip Guston, Harold Weston, Magafan sisters, Seymour Fogel, Richmond Barthé, and others)
cases.artist: Ben Shahn, Philip Guston, Harold Weston, Ethel and Jenne Magafan, Seymour Fogel, Richmond Barthé, and others
cases.institution: Wilbur J. Cohen Federal Building; Robert C. Weaver Federal Building (HUD HQ); GSA Regional Office Building (301 7th St SW); Liberty Loan Building — all Washington DC
cases.description: Trump administration GSA has flagged 46 federal buildings for 'accelerated disposal,' including four in Washington DC that preservationists consider at risk of demolition. The centerpiece is the Wilbur J. Cohen Federal Building (former SSA headquarters, 'Sistine Chapel of the New Deal'), housing integral fresco murals by Ben Shahn (The Meaning of Social Security), Philip Guston (Reconstruction and the Wellbeing of the Family), Magafan sisters, and others. Because many works are painted directly on walls, demolition would destroy them permanently. The GSA Fine Arts Collection includes 26,000 works, ~23,000 from the New Deal era. Senators Whitehouse and Schumer sent inquiry letter; 400+ artists/historians signed preservation petition; Joyce Kozloff, Martha Rosler, and Eve Ensler wrote to the Jewish Museum (which responded supportively). Preservation groups filed suit. Art Newspaper reported February 2026. GSA added the 301 7th St SW building (Harold Weston 22-panel mural cycle) to list April 10, 2026.
cases.outcome: Cohen building still occupied as of early 2026; required to be sold within 2 years of vacating (per Congressional mandate in water bill). GSA has engaged art conservation professionals to assess New Deal art condition. Preservation lawsuit (Cultural Heritage Partners v. Trump) active in DC district court — retired GSA official's declaration specifically mentions demolition as near-term possibility. No demolition yet. Staff being moved out gradually. [FOLLOW-UP PENDING]
cases.tags: Architectural preservation, Removal, Demolition, Funding dispute, Political interference, Historical erasure, Labor dispute
cases.notes:
[FOLLOW-UP PENDING] Connects the Trump architectural pattern (White House East Wing demolished, Kennedy Center mothballed, triumphal arch approved) to the destruction of integral New Deal murals — the most democratic public art program in US history, deliberately made for working people rather than elite collectors. Guston's auditorium screen is physically engineered into the room's mechanism; removing it destroys it. The Shahn murals literally teach the rationale for Social Security. Former GSA staffer: 'I think all four buildings are in real danger of being demolished without any notice, just like the East Wing of the White House.' Trump jackhammered Art Deco reliefs from Bonwit Teller in 1980 to avoid delays — the precedent is his own documented behavior. Connects to entries 019 (THPO funding elimination), 034 (NEA grant cancellations), 005/020/038 (Kennedy Center, renovation lawsuits, triumphal arch). cases.title: Exhibition catalogues ("Music Is Black"; "Fabergé: Romance to Revolution")
cases.artist: Gus Casely-Hayford (introduction author); multiple exhibition artists
cases.institution: Victoria and Albert Museum, London
cases.description: The Victoria and Albert Museum removed maps and images from at least two exhibition catalogues at the request of its Chinese printer, C&C Offset Printing, which cited China's General Administration of Press and Publication (GAPP). Deleted content included a 1930s British imperial trade route map (flagged merely because it showed China's borders) and an image of Lenin. Internal emails showed staff confusion — 'it's a historic map showing British colonial rule so nothing to do with China — just shows China on the map and that seems to be enough to warrant rejection!' — but the museum proceeded, saying edits were 'minor.' Guardian FOI investigation published April 14–15, 2026 revealed the practice. British Museum (chaired by former Chancellor George Osborne) declined to answer questions about its own Chinese-printed publications. Tate and British Library said they use Chinese printers but have not changed content.
cases.outcome: Catalogues already printed with censored content. No retraction by V&A.
cases.tags: Censorship, Political interference, Self-censorship, Institutional risk
cases.notes: Paradigm case for what The Conversation calls 'externalised censorship' — no government order, just a procurement decision and cost pressure (Chinese printers charge half of UK rates) creating a conduit for Beijing's censorship apparatus into British museum publishing. The V&A's framing of deletion as 'minor' is itself a case study in institutional self-justification. The map wasn't flagged for content about China — it was flagged because China appeared on it. Connects to entry 025 (Bangkok exhibition, Chinese diplomatic pressure) and entry 029 (China performing arts pre-production monitoring). A new category: censorship via supply chain rather than direct state action. The Osborne/British Museum angle is worth watching — Osborne championed UK-China 'golden decade' ties and the BM refused to answer questions.
cases.interested_parties: V&A / Gus Casely-Hayford (V&A East director), C&C Offset Printing (HK), China's GAPP, Guardian (reporter), British Museum, Tate, British Library, UK publishers

cases.title: Trump Triumphal Arch (proposed), Columbia Island, Washington DC
cases.institution: Columbia Island / Arlington Memorial Bridge approach, Washington DC
cases.description: President Trump is pursuing construction of a 250-foot triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery, on the Potomac side of the Lincoln Memorial. The arch originated from a 2025 proposal by architecture critic Catesby Leigh (Claremont Institute) calling for a non-'huge' arch of no more than 60 feet. Under Trump the project quadrupled: 76 feet → 164 feet (to surpass Arc de Triomphe) → 250 feet (to mark America's 250th anniversary). When asked by a CBS reporter whom the monument was for, Trump replied: 'Me.' Architect Charbonneau's design features gold eagles and lions. The Commission of Fine Arts (Trump appointees) was scheduled to review April 17. NEH has reserved $15M; total cost unspecified. Vietnam War veterans sued to block construction, citing the Commemorative Works Act of 1986 and arguing it obstructs sightlines between Lincoln Memorial and Arlington Cemetery. The Trump administration claims 1920s congressional authority for 'two tall columns' on Columbia Island suffices. Even original proponent Leigh now objects: 'It's way too big for that site.' Historian Sarah Bond: 'Trump is using Washington DC as emperors used Rome.'
cases.outcome: Commission of Fine Arts approved concept April 16, 2026 (5 of 7 Trump-appointed members present; unanimous vote among present). 100% of ~1,000 public comments opposed. Design revisions requested (remove Lady Liberty figure and eagles atop arch; reconsider lions). NEPA and NHPA reviews still required — these require public input and stakeholder consultation including Arlington National Cemetery, NPS, and DC SHPO. Veterans group lawsuit active. Groundbreaking timeline unconfirmed.
cases.tags: Design controversy, Architectural preservation, Political art, Legal challenge, Funding dispute, Landmark dispute
cases.notes:
Extraordinary convergence of Theme 1 (what counts as art/monument), Theme 2 (public funding — NEH money for a presidential vanity project while NEA grants are cut), and Theme 9 (public objection including from the project's own originator). The CBS exchange — 'Whom is this for?' / 'Me.' — is a teaching gift. Bond's Rome/emperor framing is the scholarly anchor. The pattern of Trump inflating every proposal matches the Kennedy Center and White House ballroom cases. The Commemorative Works Act fight is a direct parallel to the Philadelphia slavery exhibit (007) — both hinge on whether the executive can bypass existing legal frameworks for public commemorative space. Compare: other recent triumphal arch builders include North Korea, Indonesia, and Iraq. Architecture as autocratic signaling.

cases.description: During the US-Israel military conflict with Iran beginning February 28, 2026, cultural heritage sites have been damaged or destroyed on multiple sides. cases.title: Post-Orbán de-politicization of Hungarian cultural institutions
cases.institution: Hungarian Academy of Arts, National Film Institute, Budapest museums, public broadcaster (multiple)
cases.description: Viktor Orbán's Fidesz-KDNP party was defeated in a landslide on April 13, 2026 by Péter Magyar's Tisza party, ending 16 years of rule. During that period Orbán systematically centralized cultural institutions, gave the conservative Hungarian Academy of Arts (MMA) unprecedented grant-allocation powers, purged independent curators and museum directors, restricted LGBTQ+ content in cultural programming (2021 law used to fire Hungarian National Museum director in 2023), and aligned arts funding with Christian-nationalist ideology. Arts community celebrating. Hungarian art scene now faces what Hyperallergic describes as a 'watershed moment' comparable to 1989. Tisza has a projected two-thirds supermajority giving it power to rewrite laws governing cultural institutions. Film commissioner Csaba Káel (National Film Institute) already announced departure. Public broadcaster leadership expected to change quickly. Hungarian Academy of Arts' role expected to be reformed. Artists who boycotted co-opted institutions now face decisions about re-engagement. Tisza cultural program currently vague but promises 'institutional autonomy.'
cases.outcome: Fidesz defeated; Tisza governing. The May 31, 2026 voluntary-resignation deadline for Orbán-era appointees (incl. cultural-institution heads) passed without high-profile resignations — President Tamás Sulyok refused, citing the Venice Commission. De-Orbánization shifting toward constitutional-removal mechanisms. Cultural-institution-director turnover still unresolved as of June 1, 2026. Ongoing transition. (See 036-W.)
cases.tags: Political interference, Institutional crisis, Censorship, Funding dispute, Self-censorship
cases.notes: [FOLLOW-UP PENDING: 13 days to May 31 first hard accountability date. Fabényi still listed as director. If she does not step aside by May 31, Magyar has said legal removal will follow. This is the tracker's governance hypothesis test case: can illiberal arts-sector capture be reversed? GOVERNANCE NOTE: Hungary transitioning from illiberal capture toward democratic norms.

cases.title: Loi-cadre sur la restitution des biens culturels spoliés durant la colonisation
cases.institution: Assemblée nationale, Paris; French museums (Quai Branly, Louvre, etc.)
cases.description: French National Assembly unanimously passed (170 votes) a framework law on April 13, 2026 to facilitate return of cultural property looted from the colonial empire. Law applies to objects acquired between 1815 and 1972. Requests must pass a bilateral scientific committee (French and country-of-origin researchers) and a parliamentary commission. National Rally wanted to limit restitution to countries with 'cordial' relations with France — amendment failed. Countries with pending requests include Mali, Algeria, and Benin. Culture Minister Catherine Pégard: the law 'opens a new page of our History.' Completes 2023 framework laws covering Nazi-looted property and human remains.
cases.outcome: Assemblée nationale passed amended text unanimously April 13-14. CMP (commission mixte paritaire) PENDING — required because AN amended the Sénat text. Not yet promulgated. CMP must reconcile both chambers' versions before final adoption.
cases.tags: Repatriation, Colonial legacy, Legislative action, Ethical museum
cases.notes: Major legislative milestone — first comprehensive French repatriation framework law covering colonial-era objects broadly. Connects directly to entry 015/015-A (European human remains repatriation). The 1815–1972 date range is notable: starts with the Second Colonial Empire; ends with the 1972 UNESCO convention. RN's 'cordial relations' amendment reveals the political fault line — repatriation as leverage. Sarr-Savoy 2018 report (commissioned by Macron, Ouagadougou speech) finally bearing institutional fruit. Theme 5 capstone entry.

cases.title: European museum collections of human remains / colonial repatriation
cases.institution: Museum Vrolik (Amsterdam), UK museums (263,000+ items), German museums, French institutions
cases.description: NYT feature on European museums confronting colonial-era human remains. Central case: Museum Vrolik in Amsterdam, where Dutch customs official Menucha Latumaerissa tracked down Moluccan skulls taken from Amtufu village in 1912 by a Dutch colonial army medical officer. Skulls had been used for 'race science' — craniometry and anthropometry to invent racial hierarchies justifying colonial subjugation. Skulls now repatriated; empty stands displayed in exhibition 'Imagine: The Future of Human Remains from Colonial Contexts' (through Jun 2027). Broader European pattern: Karolinska Institute (Stockholm) repatriated 122 skulls since 2015 but can't identify origins of many more. Berlin Museum of Prehistory spent $4M researching 1,500+ skulls — some African countries declined repatriation due to political obstacles. Charité hospital (Berlin) repatriated 216 remains since 2011 across 10 ceremonies. No EU-wide legislation exists; US has NAGPRA (1990) but Europe relies on patchwork of local laws. Germany creating Coordination Council (Apr 2026). France Senate passed framework (Jan 2026).
cases.outcome: Ongoing. Germany creating formal council. France passed framework. UK debating legislation. Netherlands has active repatriation program. No single resolution — this is a continental-scale institutional reckoning.
cases.tags: Repatriation, Colonial legacy, Ethical museum, Human remains, Legislative action
cases.notes: Latumaerissa's quote is devastating: 'The Dutch destroyed everything of ours, our language, our culture. First they forbid it, and we all had to become Christians and learn the Dutch language, and then they displayed and traded our ancestors' skulls.' And: 'They studied our people for racial science... I don't know why they did that. You could also just ask us. You can appreciate our culture, our language, our traditions. Isn't that enough?' The empty stands as exhibition design — showing absence rather than presence — is a powerful curatorial choice. Berlin's experience where African governments blocked family requests for repatriation adds a layer of complexity your students should wrestle with. Latumaerissa is now pursuing the return of a baby skeleton from the Aru Islands taken in 1929. Theme 5 at its deepest. Enrich Wednesday with Dutch, German, French sources.
cases.interested_parties: Menucha Latumaerissa (Moluccan diaspora researcher), Laurens de Rooy (Museum Vrolik director), Steph Scholten (ICOM board), Eva Ahren (Karolinska), Bernhard Heeb (Berlin Museum of Prehistory), Thomas Schnalke (Charité), Jos van Beurden (Free University Amsterdam), descendant communities in Moluccan archipelago/Tanimbar/Aru Islands
cases.coverage_geography: Netherlands, UK, Germany, France, Indonesia, New Zealand, West Africa

cases.title: AztLÁn, túnel del tiempo
cases.artist: 33 Chicano artists including Alexa Ramírez, 3B Collective, Chaz Bojorquez
cases.institution: Museo del Palacio de Bellas Artes, Mexico City
cases.description: Exhibition framed as resistance to erasure of Mexican-American history under second Trump administration. Features work addressing deportation (nearly 190,000 under Trump's second term), family separation, and border politics. Curator Joshua Sánchez calls it 'settling a historic debt' with Chicano art tradition. References 1932 whitewashing of Siqueiros's 'América tropical' mural as historical precedent for current erasure.
cases.outcome: Exhibition currently open.
cases.tags: Political art, Historical erasure, Migration, Resistance
cases.notes: Not a controversy in the traditional sense — this is art responding to the censorship pattern documented in entries 007 (Philadelphia), 011 (UNT/Marka27), and 012 (Smithsonian). The Siqueiros 'América tropical' reference is extraordinary — mural whitewashed in 1932 for criticizing US imperialism, now invoked in 2026 as artists face a new wave of the same erasure. Connects US federal censorship to Latin American artistic resistance across nearly a century.
cases.interested_parties: Museo del Palacio de Bellas Artes, Joshua Sánchez (chief curator), Alexa Ramírez, 3B Collective, EFE (wire service)
cases.coverage_geography: Mexico, US (subject matter), Latin America (wire coverage via EFE/Infobae)

cases.title: Venice Biennale Visitors' Lions / legal threat
cases.artist: 100+ artists in 'In Minor Keys' and national pavilions
cases.institution: 61st Venice Biennale, Venice, Italy
cases.description: As of June 3–4, 2026: more than 100 artists (67 from main exhibition 'In Minor Keys,' 39 from national pavilions) published an open letter on e-flux announcing 'next steps towards legal action' against the Biennale Foundation. The artists allege their formal requests (sent May 9 and again May 20) to be removed from the Visitors' Lions ballot received neither reply nor acknowledgment. On May 14, the Biennale emailed ticketed visitors inviting them to vote from a list still including the withdrawing artists. The Biennale's May 28 response stated it would keep names on the ballot 'to guarantee all visitors freedom of expression' but claimed votes for withdrawing artists would not be counted. The artists called this 'a waste of time.' No lawsuit has been filed as of the scan date.
cases.outcome: Legal threat issued. Ballot unchanged as of June 4. Visitors' Lions results expected before Biennale closes late September.
cases.tags: Legal challenge, Geopolitics, Institutional crisis, Political art
cases.notes: [FOLLOW-UP PENDING] The Visitors' Lions announcement is expected November 22, 2026. Key questions: (1) Will the Biennale remove withdrawing artists' names from the ballot before that date; (2) Will any formal lawsuit be filed before November; (3) What legal theory grounds the claim — right of publicity, moral rights, misrepresentation? The Biennale's position — 'your name stays but votes don't count' — is legally and institutionally strange: it treats inclusion in a public ballot as a form of expressive freedom the institution exercises on behalf of visitors, over the artist's explicit objection. This is analytically close to the VARA moral-rights framework. The scale of solidarity (100+ artists, international pavilions) makes this the most significant collective legal threat in Biennale history.
cases.interested_parties: La Biennale Foundation; withdrawing artists (100+); Biennale visitors; Koyo Kouoh (late curator); resigned jury; Italian culture ministry

cases.title: Trump Kennedy Center Renaming / Artist Boycott
cases.institution: John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, Washington DC
cases.description: Trump-appointed board renamed the Kennedy Center after Trump in Dec 2025, added his name to exterior signage. Dozens of artists canceled performances including Philip Glass, Renée Fleming, Hamilton, Martha Graham Dance Company, SF Ballet. Washington National Opera severed ties. Kennedy Center threatened $1M lawsuit against jazz musician Chuck Redd for canceling. Trump announced 2-year closure from Jul 2026. Congresswoman Beatty sued to reverse name change.
cases.outcome: Core claims resolved May 29, 2026 (Cooper summary judgment): renaming blocked and Trump name/signage to be removed within two weeks; planned two-year closure blocked; Beatty's ex officio voting rights restored; D.C. Preservation League parallel challenge denied. Renovations may proceed; Board could revote on closure with proper process. Trump signaled transfer of control to Congress. See 005-AB. Appeal possible; artist-boycott context ongoing. UPDATE (June 11–12, 2026): Board voted to appeal; Cooper denied stay June 12; administration appealed to D.C. Circuit (see 005-AH).
cases.tags: Political interference, Censorship, Funding dispute, Institutional crisis, Legal challenge
cases.notes: Resolved: Cooper issued the long-awaited summary judgment on May 29, 2026 — renaming blocked, closure blocked, Beatty voting rights restored. See 005-AB. cases.title: Ladies Lounge
cases.institution: Museum of Old and New Art (MONA), Hobart, Tasmania
cases.description: Women-only art installation barring male entry prompted discrimination complaint from visitor Jason Lau. Tribunal ruled it discriminatory; MONA closed it rather than admit men. Supreme Court overturned ruling, finding the work promoted equal opportunity by creating a 'flipped universe.' Reopened for victory lap Dec 2024–Jan 2025.
cases.outcome: Resolved in MONA's favor. Lounge reopened for final run, then closed.
cases.tags: Legal challenge, Gender, Discrimination law, Art-as-provocation
cases.notes: Fascinating test case for whether exclusion can be art. Court accepted that pointing out hypocrisy was a valid artistic purpose. Kaechele released commemorative fragrance called 'The Verdict.'
cases.interested_parties: Kirsha Kaechele, David Walsh (MONA founder), Jason Lau (complainant), Acting Justice Shane Marshall

cases.title: Louvre Crown Jewels Heist / Institutional Crisis
cases.institution: Musée du Louvre, Galerie d'Apollon
cases.description: Thieves stole 8 pieces of French Crown Jewels valued at €88M in an 8-minute daylight heist. Exposed systemic security failures, chronic understaffing. 420+ staff went on strike. Director Laurence des Cars resigned Feb 2026. Empress Eugénie's crown, dropped by thieves, now being restored.
cases.outcome: 4 suspects arrested; jewels still missing. Director resigned. Empress Eugénie's crown restoration underway. Investigation has international dimension: phone analysis links Eastern European suspects to Belgium; French police pursued lead there (June 2026; see ACI-002-C). Film adaptation announced (Romain Gavras).
cases.tags: Security failure, Labor dispute, Institutional crisis
cases.notes: Not traditional art controversy but major institutional failure. Raises questions about museum obligations to collections vs. revenue/attendance priorities.
cases.interested_parties: Laurence des Cars (director, resigned), Union syndicale Solidaires, Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau, Macron administration
